about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This document is a U.S. Government Accountability Office report to congressional committees, issued September 17, 2008, examining (1) changes and challenges in the fiscal year 2009 overseas master plans, the extent to which they address prior GAO recommendations, and the plans' timeliness; and (2) the status of DOD's master planning efforts for the proposed military buildup on Guam, including the working-level plan, environmental impact statement, and associated challenges.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The fiscal year 2009 overseas master plans generally reflect recent changes in U.S. basing strategies and implementation challenges, and address most of GAO's prior recommendations, except the U.S. Pacific Command plan does not describe Air Force training challenges in South Korea. DOD provided the plans to Congress in May 2008, three months after the February 2008 budget submission, despite the requirement to issue them with the budget submission. DOD has established a framework for the military buildup on Guam but has not issued the congressionally required comprehensive master plan, initially due December 2006 and extended to September 2008; a working-level plan is to be submitted by the 2008 deadline but is a one-time snapshot that DOD officials said will not be considered a master plan. The environmental impact statement and record of decision are not expected until December 2009 and January 2010, and DOD officials expect a comprehensive master plan within 90 days after the record of decision. DOD has not fully identified funding requirements, faces operational and training challenges, and the buildup is expected to have significant impact on Guam's community and public infrastructure.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: About 8,000 Marines and an estimated 9,000 dependents are tentatively planned to move from Okinawa, Japan, to Guam by 2014. The buildup is estimated to increase Guam's current population of 171,000 by an estimated 25,000 active duty military personnel and dependents (14.6 percent) to 196,000. The total cost of all services' realignments on Guam is estimated to be more than $13 billion; the Marine Corps buildup is estimated to cost $10.3 billion, and Marine Forces Pacific officials recently estimated the Marine Corps realignment alone will exceed $15 billion. The government of Japan is expected to contribute a total of $6.09 billion, of which up to $2.8 billion would be funds without reimbursement and another $3.3 billion in loans and equity investments. The fiscal year 2009 military construction budget submission includes approximately $24.4 billion for military construction and family housing, of which nearly $1.1 billion (4.7 percent) is designated for specific overseas locations. The U.S. European Command identified over $284 million in facility requirements to support the ballistic missile defense program in the Czech Republic. The U.S. Central Command identified a goal of $1.7 billion in host nation funding. U.S. Pacific Command reported reducing major U.S. installations in South Korea from 41 to 10 (76 percent). The Japanese Facilities Improvement Program decreased from an estimated $1 billion in 1993 to $242 million. The U.S. government received approximately $656 million in residual value and payment-in-kind compensation since 1989. Training ranges for the Marine Corps in Guam and the Northern Mariana Islands are estimated to cost $2 billion. Strategic lift operating from Guam will cost an estimated additional $88 million annually compared with Okinawa. A July 2008 study estimated annual construction capacity at approximately $1 billion to $1.5 billion, potentially $2.5 billion, versus more than $3 billion per year needed. Preliminary analysis indicates 15,000 to 20,000 construction workers will be required, and Guam may meet only 10 to 15 percent locally. The Governor of Guam testified the government of Guam will need $6.1 billion for infrastructure upgrades. The ballistic missile defense task force is approximately 630 soldiers and an estimated 950 dependents.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The report recommends that the Secretary of Defense direct the Under Secretary of Defense for Acquisition, Technology and Logistics to initiate a process of developing global defense posture updates earlier each year so DOD can provide the congressional defense committees the overseas planning report with the administration's annual budget submission, and direct the Executive Director of the Joint Guam Program Office to provide the congressional defense committees with annual updates of the Guam working-level plan until a comprehensive master plan is finalized and submitted to Congress. DOD partially agreed with the first recommendation and agreed with the second.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The report states that DOD has not yet developed a comprehensive master plan for Guam; the environmental impact statement and record of decision are not expected until December 2009 and January 2010, respectively, and many key decisions on location, size, and makeup of infrastructure depend on them. Plans for the detailed force composition of units relocating to Guam, associated facility requirements, and implications for other services' realignments continue to be refined; no decision has been made on whether to deploy additional forces under the Grow the Force initiative. DOD has not fully identified all funding requirements, including costs of other defense organizations and training ranges, and uncertainties exist in the cost-sharing arrangement with Japan. Existing training ranges on Guam are not sufficient, and operational challenges such as sealift and airlift capabilities remain. The effects on Guam's community and public infrastructure have yet to be fully addressed, and the government of Guam has not identified sufficient resources. Also, no requirement exists to report periodically on DOD's planning efforts after the working-level plan is submitted in September 2008.

audience.name: Who it is for
audience.text: The report is addressed to the congressional committees, specifically the Senate and House Armed Services Committees and the Senate and House Appropriations Committees and their defense subcommittees, to inform oversight and funding decisions on DOD's overseas planning and the Guam military buildup.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This GAO report (GAO-08-1138, issued September 17, 2008, 27 pages) provides an update on the Department of Health and Human Services' efforts to define and implement an overall privacy approach for electronic personal health information exchanged within a nationwide health information network, following a January 2007 GAO recommendation. It assesses the Office of the National Coordinator for Health IT initiatives against key HIPAA privacy principles and challenges to nationwide health information exchange, and concludes that HHS has taken important steps but has not fully implemented an overall privacy approach.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The findings are GAO's own. Since January 2007, HHS has undertaken various initiatives contributing to an overall privacy approach: the Healthcare Information Technology Standards Panel defined standards for implementing security features; the Certification Commission for Healthcare Information Technology defined certification criteria including privacy protections; state-level initiatives convened stakeholders to propose solutions; the Office of the National Coordinator identified milestones and assigned responsibility for integrating outcomes; and the Secretary released a federal health IT strategic plan in June 2008 with privacy and security objectives, strategies, and target dates. However, HHS has not defined a process for ensuring that all privacy principles and challenges will be fully and adequately addressed, so the department has not fully implemented GAO's recommendation. In the absence of such a process, HHS faces the risk that privacy protection measures may not be consistently and effectively built into health IT programs, jeopardizing patient privacy and public confidence and trust.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: The report is GAO-08-1138, issued September 17, 2008, and has 27 pages. A September 2007 survey sponsored by the Institute of Medicine indicated that nearly 60 percent of respondents did not believe that the privacy of personal medical records and health information was adequately protected by federal and state laws and organization practices. In April 2004, President Bush issued an executive order calling for a strategic plan for interoperable health IT. In 2005, the department awarded four health IT contracts. In January 2007, four test network implementations, or prototypes, demonstrated potential nationwide health information exchange. In June 2008, the Secretary released a federal health IT strategic plan that includes a strategy to complete a confidentiality, privacy, and security framework by the end of 2008 and a strategy to address inconsistent statutes or regulations for the exchange of electronic health information by the end of 2011. The Office of the National Coordinator indicated that the framework is to be developed and published by the end of calendar year 2008. In February 2008, the National Committee on Vital and Health Statistics submitted five recommendations to the Secretary. In August 2007, the State Alliance for e-Health proposed five recommendations.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The document recommends that the Secretary of Health and Human Services direct the National Coordinator for Health IT to include in the department's overall privacy approach a process for assessing and prioritizing its many privacy-related initiatives and the needs of stakeholders. HHS generally agreed with the information in the report but neither agreed nor disagreed with the recommendation, and stated that it is actively pursuing a two-phased process for assessing and prioritizing privacy-related initiatives intended to build public trust and confidence in health IT.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The document states that HHS has not defined a process for ensuring that all privacy principles and challenges will be fully and adequately addressed; that without such a process some principles and challenges may be addressed extensively while others receive inadequate attention; and that HHS may not be able to ensure comprehensive coverage of all key privacy principles and challenges. It notes that recommendations from HHS's advisory groups were still under consideration by the Secretary. HHS commented that the report lists representative examples of HHS initiatives and is not intended to provide a complete compilation of HHS's privacy and security activities. The audit was conducted from April 2008 through September 2008, and GAO supplemented its analysis with interviews of officials from the National Coordinator's office.

audience.name: Who it is for
audience.text: The report is addressed to the Chairman, Subcommittee on Oversight of Government Management, the Federal Workforce, and the District of Columbia, Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs, U.S. Senate, to support congressional oversight of HHS's health information technology privacy efforts.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This document is a U.S. Government Accountability Office report (GAO-08-180, issued June 27, 2008, 79 pages) on the limitations of first responders' tools for detecting and modeling hazardous chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear (CBRN) releases in urban areas. It addresses four questions: the limitations of CBRN detection equipment currently available for first responders; what DHS has done on performance standards and testing; the limitations of plume models for tracking airborne CBRN releases in urban environments, including toxic industrial chemicals and materials; and what information is available on the effects of CBRN exposure on urban populations.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The report's key findings are that, more than six years after September 11, 2001, local first responders do not have tools that can accurately and quickly identify CBRN releases in urban environments. Radiological and nuclear detection equipment can detect the presence of materials but cannot predict atmospheric dispersion, and no federal agency has the mission to develop, independently test, and certify radiological detection equipment for first responders' use in the atmosphere. Chemical detectors are generally inadequate for detecting chemical warfare agents at less than lethal but still potentially harmful concentrations, and handheld biological assays are not always reliable; BioWatch does not provide real-time results. As of October 30, 2007, DHS had adopted only 4 standards for CBRN detection equipment and none for chemical or biological detection equipment, and DHS does not independently test manufacturers' claims. Plume models commonly used for emergency response have not been adequately validated for complex urban environments and can produce contradictory results, as TOPOFF exercises showed; urban plume models have unpredictable uncertainty and cannot determine source terms with certainty. Significant data gaps exist on how CBRN releases affect heterogeneous urban populations, especially vulnerable groups.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: The report reports the following figures, among others. In the 2001 anthrax attack, 22 persons contracted anthrax disease and 5 died in four states and Washington, D.C. In one planning scenario, a sarin release in three city office buildings is estimated to kill 6,000 people and cause $300 million in economic damages. Nine of 15 projected homeland security threat scenarios involve CBRN agents or toxic industrial materials in metropolitan areas. Approximately 800,000 shipments of hazardous materials travel daily throughout the United States. The 1984 Bhopal release killed approximately 3,800 people. In the January 6, 2005, Graniteville, South Carolina, accident, 11,500 gallons of chlorine gas were released, 9 people died, 8 from inhaling chlorine gas, at least 529 sought medical care, and 5,453 residents were evacuated within a mile of the collision. Real-time detection has been defined as 30 seconds or less from the time potential material reaches the device until an alarm is triggered. BioWatch has more than 30 participating jurisdictions, cost about $236 million in fiscal years 2005 to 2007, collects samples on filters every 24 hours, tests for six biothreat pathogens, and does not identify a threat agent until several hours to more than a day after release. DHS S&T assessed IMS and SAW sensitivity for V and G nerve agents as approximately 2 parts per billion to 20 parts per billion, with a detection limit of 200 to 300 parts per billion for blister agents; electrochemical cells can detect from parts per billion to low parts per million. Handheld immunoassays yield results in approximately 15 minutes. As of October 30, 2007, DHS had adopted 39 total standards, of which 4 were for radiation and nuclear detection equipment and none for chemical or biological detection equipment. Equipment standards generally take 3 to 5 years to develop, while DHS noted radiation detection and powder sampling standards were developed in 12 to 18 months. In Washington State, CBRN detection equipment was acquired with about $3.2 million of SHSP and UASI grant funds in 2004-2005; Seattle alone spent about $500,000; Connecticut spent about $1.8 million in 2003-2005. One brand of digital dosimeters tested in Washington State consistently read only 40 percent of what current dosimeters read. As of October 2007, DHS's Responder Knowledge Base included 1,127 certifications and 268 reports of operational suitability testing. An August 2002 OFCM study evaluated 29 modeling systems, and OFCM stated that most of the more than 140 documented modeling systems are limited in their ability to predict plume path and contamination in urban environments. CAMEO includes a database with information on over 6,000 chemicals, and ALOHA does not make predictions for distances greater than 6.2 miles (10 kilometers) from the release point or for more than an hour after a release begins. NARAC and IMAAC can provide an automated prediction for CBRN events within 5 to 15 minutes. The TOPOFF exercises were held May 20-24, 2000; May 12-16, 2003; April 4-8, 2005; and October 15-20, 2007.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The report recommends that the Secretary of Homeland Security take four executive actions: (1) reach agreement with DOD, DOE, EPA, and other agencies involved with developing, testing, and certifying CBRN detection equipment on which agency should have the missions and responsibilities to develop, independently test, and certify detection equipment that first responders can use to detect hazardous material releases in the atmosphere; (2) ensure that manufacturers' claims are independently tested and validated regarding whether their commercial off-the-shelf CBRN detection equipment can detect given hazardous material at specific sensitivities; (3) refine IMAAC's procedures by working with other federal, state, and local agencies to develop common/joint IMAAC emergency response practices, including procedures for dealing with contradictory plume modeling information, refine the concept of operations for chemical, biological, and radiological releases, and delineate the type and scale of major CBRN incidents that would qualify for IMAAC assistance; and (4) in conjunction with IMAAC, work with the federal plume modeling community to accelerate research and development to address plume model deficiencies in urban areas and improve federal modeling and assessment capabilities, including improvements to meteorological information, plume models, and data sets to evaluate plume models. The report notes that DHS concurred with the recommendations and that DOC proposed, and GAO included, the recommendation on accelerating research and development on plume model deficiencies.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The report does not settle which agency should have the mission to develop, test, and certify radiological detection equipment for first responders, and it states that no agency now has that mission. It also states that GAO did not independently evaluate what CBRN technologies may have been evaluated under DHS's Domestic Preparedness Program or EPA's Environmental Technologies Verification Program, and did not independently evaluate the SAVER assessments. The report notes that DHS's observations about current chemical detectors were based partly on anecdotal information and manufacturers' claims that in some cases have been independently tested and evaluated; that manufacturers of handheld immunoassays expressed concern about the 2002 CDC/FBI evaluation study's methods, objectivity, and overall quality; and that the detector guides available to first responders do not contain testing data validating manufacturers' claims. It also states that TOPOFF exercises were limited by the use of canned weather patterns, that TOPOFF 2 results were affected by exercise artificiality and improper generation and interpretation of simulated data, that source-term information may be unavailable or based on uncertain and incomplete data that cannot be confirmed, and that many users assume plume models are more accurate than warranted.

audience.name: Who it is for
audience.text: The intended audience is the congressional requesters, including the chairmen and ranking members of the Senate Appropriations Committee, Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, House Energy and Commerce Committee, and House Appropriations Subcommittee on Homeland Security, and the report supports congressional oversight and legislative decisions on first responders' CBRN detection and modeling capabilities.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This document is a GAO report to a U.S. Senate subcommittee on undisbursed balances remaining in expired federal grant accounts. It analyzes quarterly closeout data from 2003 through 2006 for the Department of Health and Human Services' Payment Management System, the largest civilian federal grant payment system, which handled about 70 percent of federal grant disbursements in 2006, and it reviews audit reports and agency Performance and Accountability Reports to identify the causes of grant closeout problems and actions agencies have taken to address them.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The report finds that about $1 billion in undisbursed funding remained in expired grant accounts in PMS during calendar year 2006, representing about 1 percent of total funds made available for all expired grant accounts in PMS during that year and, when only accounts with undisbursed balances were considered, about 26 percent on average of the original funding made available. The quarterly amount of undisbursed funding in expired grant accounts increased from about $600 million in 2003 to about $1 billion during 2006. Expired grant accounts with undisbursed funds were associated with thousands of grantees in over 325 different federal grant programs. The accounts with the largest undisbursed balances shared certain characteristics: midsize funding awards from over $100,000 to $100 million, project-based awards, and state grantees. The report also finds that audit reports and agency Performance and Accountability Reports showed undisbursed balances in expired grant accounts were a long-standing challenge, with causes including closeouts as a low management priority, inconsistent closeout procedures, poorly timed communications with grantees, and insufficient compliance or enforcement. When agencies such as HHS, DOJ, and EPA made concerted efforts, auditors reported improvements in the timeliness of grant closeouts and reductions in undisbursed funding. The report further finds that current OMB circulars do not instruct federal departments and agencies to track and report on expired grants and undisbursed grant funding.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: Federal grant awards to nonfederal entities increased from $300 billion to over $450 billion from 2000 through 2006, and grants represent about one-sixth of the federal budget. In calendar year 2006, about $1 billion in undisbursed funding remained in expired grant accounts in PMS, which handled about 70 percent of all federal grant disbursements in 2006; this represented about 1 percent of total funds made available for all expired grant accounts in PMS during 2006, but about 26 percent on average of original funding when only accounts with undisbursed balances were considered. Quarterly undisbursed amounts rose from about $600 million in 2003 to about $1 billion during 2006; among expired accounts with undisbursed balances, the average was 14 to 16 percent of funds made available from March 2003 through March 2005 and 24 to 26 percent from June 2005 through December 2006. More than 325 different federal grant programs and thousands of grantees were involved, and in 15 of 16 quarters at least four federal departments using PMS had over 100 expired grant accounts with undisbursed funding. The largest balances were in midsize grants with original funding awards from over $100,000 to $100 million, project-based grants, and state grantees. The report reviewed over 150 related audit reports. EPA closed out only 37 percent of grants in fiscal year 2005 within 180 days. DOJ's OIG reported in 2006 that $172 million in undisbursed funding could have been deobligated. Operation Closeout closed 4,136 grants, resulting in over $30 million in deobligated funds; OJP reduced its backlog of expired grants from 11,356 to 6,237 from 2001 to 2005, shortened its closeout timeline from 180 days to 120 days, and reduced response time to grant adjustment requests by 10 days. EPA nearly eliminated its backlog of over 23,000 expired grants accumulated between 1999 and 2003. HHS's 2006 PAR reported more than 64,000 grants with a remaining balance of $1.6 billion eligible for closeout, 75 percent of which had been expired for more than 2 years. EPA set a goal of 90 percent grant closure in 2005 and reported a 95 percent grant closure rate in its 2006 PAR. PMS processed over $320 billion in payments to grant recipients in 2006, contained over 200,000 open grants as of June 2007, and open grants in PMS represented over $1.3 trillion in total funding as of May 2007.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The report recommends that the Director of the Office of Management and Budget instruct all executive departments and independent agencies to take two actions: annually track the amount of undisbursed grant funding remaining in expired grant accounts, and report on the status and resolution of the undisbursed funding in their annual performance plan and in their annual Performance and Accountability Report, including the amount of undisbursed grant funding in expired grant accounts, why these funds were undisbursed, the actions taken to resolve the undisbursed funding and close the expired grants and related accounts, and outcomes associated with these actions.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The report states several limitations and open questions. The results for expired grant accounts in PMS could not be compared to program characteristics for all closed federal grants or all closed grants using PMS, due to the burden of collecting comparable data from the eight other federal civilian payment systems or from all closed grants in PMS, so the report cannot know whether the program characteristics represented a disproportionate share. The analysis was limited to expired grant accounts with undisbursed balances listed in PMS closeout reports from 2003 through 2006, and it excluded grant accounts without specific time limits, such as TANF and Medicaid, as well as certain block grants and accounts without identifiable program descriptions. The report notes that each program characteristic analysis was independent and cannot be combined into a general statement, and that it did not interview policy experts or agency grant managers to explore why expired grants with different program characteristics might have larger undisbursed balances. It also states that current OMB circulars do not explicitly instruct agencies to track or report undisbursed balances in expired grant accounts, and OMB's comments did not indicate a commitment to implement the recommendations; OMB said it does not favor requiring agencies to report these balances in their PARs.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This document is a U.S. Government Accountability Office report (GAO-08-525, issued June 27, 2008) to congressional requesters on federal agency efforts to encrypt sensitive information. It examines how commercially available encryption technologies can help federal agencies protect sensitive information and reduce risks, the federal laws, policies, and guidance governing encryption use, and the extent to which 24 major federal agencies had implemented or planned to implement encryption technologies to protect sensitive information, including testing of encryption practices at six selected agencies.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The report's own findings are that many commercially available encryption technologies exist to protect stored and transmitted data, but implementing them incorrectly can create a false sense of security or render data inaccessible. Federal laws do not specifically require encryption but provide a framework, and OMB policy recommended in 2006 and required in 2007 that agencies encrypt data on mobile computers and devices and use NIST-approved cryptographic modules. All 24 surveyed agencies had initiated encryption efforts, but none had completed them or documented comprehensive implementation plans; encryption of stored information on mobile devices lagged behind encryption of transmitted information, with agencies reporting that about 70 percent of laptop computers and handheld devices had not been encrypted. Testing at six agencies found weaknesses in installing and configuring FIPS-validated cryptographic modules, monitoring encryption effectiveness, developing and documenting encryption policies and procedures, and training personnel, and the report concludes that federal information may remain at increased risk of unauthorized disclosure, loss, and modification.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: Reported figures include the following: the 2006 Department of Veterans Affairs breach involved a laptop and external hard drive containing the personal information of approximately 26.5 million veterans and U.S. military personnel. Agency-reported breaches include a stolen laptop containing personally identifiable information for as many as 4,000 participants in the Marine Corps New Parent Support Program in February 2008, and a missing external hard drive containing personal data for 100,000 archived employment records at the Transportation Security Administration in May 2007. Incidents reported to US-CERT increased from 3,634 in fiscal year 2005 to 5,503 in fiscal year 2006 and 13,029 in fiscal year 2007, about a 259 percent increase. In the July through September 2007 survey of 24 major federal agencies, 8 agencies reported encrypting information on less than 20 percent of laptops and handheld devices, 5 between 20 and 39 percent, 2 between 40 and 59 percent, 3 between 60 and 79 percent, and 6 between 80 and 100 percent; overall, agencies reported about 70 percent of these devices had not been encrypted. Of 22 agencies, 10 reported encrypting less than 20 percent of portable storage media taken offsite and 3 reported between 20 and 39 percent; of 17 agencies, 9 reported encrypting less than 20 percent of offsite backup storage media. Six agencies reported having other storage devices that could contain sensitive data, 4 of those agencies had not encrypted these additional devices, and officials at 1 agency had no plans to encrypt sensitive data on portable media. Of 23 agencies reporting on wired Internet transmissions, 18 reported encrypting 80 to 100 percent; of 21 reporting on wireless transmissions, 12 reported encrypting 80 to 100 percent. At selected agencies, 2 of 6 had not installed FIPS-validated cryptographic modules, 4 had not configured installed encryption technologies in accordance with FIPS 140-2 specifications, all 6 had not developed or documented policies and procedures for managing encryption implementation, and 3 had not adequately trained personnel. Among tested devices, Education had not installed FIPS-validated encryption on any of 15 tested laptops; USDA, State, and GSA had installed FIPS-compliant technologies on all 58 tested laptops; NASA had installed its encryption software on 27 of 29 tested laptops; and one of Education's three virtual private networks was not FIPS-compliant.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The report makes 20 recommendations for executive action. It recommends that the Director of OMB clarify governmentwide policy requiring agencies to encrypt sensitive agency data through additional guidance and/or educational activities, and monitor the effectiveness of agencies' encryption implementation plans and efforts to inventory sensitive information. It recommends that the Secretary of Agriculture direct the chief information officer to establish a mechanism to monitor successful installation and functioning of encryption products, develop and implement departmentwide procedures for encryption key establishment and management, and develop and implement encryption training. It recommends that the Secretary of Education direct the chief information officer to evaluate, select, and install FIPS 140-compliant products for all encryption needs and document an implementation plan; configure installed FIPS-compliant encryption technologies in accordance with FIPS-validated security settings; develop and implement departmentwide policy and procedures for encryption key establishment and management; develop and implement departmentwide procedures for use of FIPS-compliant cryptography; and develop and implement encryption training. It recommends that the Secretary of Housing and Urban Development direct the chief information officer to evaluate, select, and install FIPS 140-compliant products and document an implementation plan; configure installed FIPS-compliant encryption technologies in accordance with FIPS-validated security settings; and develop and implement departmentwide procedures for FIPS-compliant cryptography and encryption key establishment and management. It recommends that the Secretary of State direct the chief information officer to develop and implement departmentwide policy and procedures for encryption key establishment and management and departmentwide procedures for use of FIPS-compliant cryptography. It makes the same two recommendations to the Administrator of the General Services Administration. It recommends that the Administrator of NASA direct the chief information officer to establish a mechanism to monitor successful installation and functioning of encryption products, develop and implement departmentwide policy and procedures for encryption key establishment and management, and develop and implement encryption training.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The document states that agencies reported uncertainty regarding the applicability of OMB's encryption requirements, and that while OMB officials said the term mobile computers and devices was intended to include all agency laptops, handheld devices, and portable storage devices, this description is not clear in any of OMB's memorandums. It also states that none of the 24 agencies had documented comprehensive encryption implementation plans, that OMB did not provide evidence that it monitored agencies' efforts to inventory sensitive information or develop implementation plans, that some agencies lacked mechanisms to detect whether encryption products were installed and functioning, and that three agencies had not enabled encryption of data stored on BlackBerry devices while awaiting a solution from the vendor. The report does not settle whether encryption will be completed or whether the identified weaknesses will be resolved.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This is a GAO report to congressional requesters assessing U.S. Customs and Border Protection's efforts to promote international supply chain security standards. It covers CBP's actions to develop and implement international standards through the World Customs Organization's SAFE Framework, CBP's actions with international partners to achieve mutual recognition of customs security practices, and issues CBP and foreign customs administrations anticipate in implementing the statutory requirement to scan 100 percent of U.S.-bound container cargo. The scope includes CBP's CSI and C-TPAT programs, WCO capacity-building efforts, mutual recognition arrangements, and the Secure Freight Initiative pilot, based on CBP documentation, interviews with U.S. and foreign officials, and visits to six CSI seaports.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The document reports that CBP took a lead role, with 11 other WCO members, in developing the SAFE Framework, which was adopted in June 2005 by the WCO's 173 member customs administrations and is based on CBP's CSI and C-TPAT programs; as of June 2008, 154 WCO member countries, including the United States, had signed letters of intent to implement it. It reports that CBP worked with international partners toward mutual recognition, signing the world's first mutual recognition arrangement with New Zealand in June 2007, later arrangements with Jordan and Canada in June 2008, and agreeing with the European Commission to establish mutual recognition of customs-to-business partnership programs by early 2009. It also reports that CBP and international partners said the statutory requirement to scan 100 percent of U.S.-bound container cargo runs counter to and could adversely affect implementation of international customs security standards, that it is unclear who will pay for the additional resources needed, and that officials were concerned it could provide a lower level of security, harm the flow of commerce, and disproportionately affect trade with developing countries.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: More than 700 foreign seaports ship cargo to the United States. Eleven million oceangoing cargo containers arrived at U.S. seaports in fiscal year 2007—roughly 30,000 oceangoing containers arrived each day that year. The WCO represented the customs administrations of 173 countries, and the SAFE Framework was adopted in June 2005 by the 173 member customs administrations. As of June 2008, 154 WCO member countries, including the United States, had signed letters of intent for implementing the SAFE Framework. CBP operated CSI at 58 seaports in 33 countries; the document says 6 of the 58 CSI seaports were visited, and 2 of the 33 countries participating in CSI—Canada and Japan—had decided to station customs officials in U.S. seaports as of July 2008. As of May 2008, there were over 8,400 C-TPAT members. As of April 2008, 111 countries were participating in the WCO capacity-building program; as of July 2008, 104 had completed the first phase, 65 had moved into the second phase, and one was in the third phase. CBP provided training and assistance to 10 countries in the capacity-building program. According to WCO data, about 70 countries have begun developing their own national AEO programs. The Booz Allen Hamilton simulation reported that seaport closures could last 12 days and result in a $58 billion loss to the U.S. economy. The 9/11 Act requires 100 percent scanning of all U.S.-bound container cargo by 2012, with possible 2-year, renewable extensions for individual seaports. The SFI pilot program was conducted at six selected CSI seaports and became operational in October 2007. CBP and the European Commission agreed to establish mutual recognition of customs-to-business partnership programs by early 2009. The U.S.-EU feeder port pilots were 6-month projects: the Port of Szczecin, Poland, from March 2007 to September 2007; the port of Aarhus, Denmark, beginning April 2008; and Salerno, Italy, beginning July 2008.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: Not stated in this document.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The document states that the SFI pilot program is still underway and its full impacts are still unknown, and that GAO had not yet fully reviewed implementation of the 100 percent scanning requirement, offering preliminary observations instead. It states that results from visits to six CSI seaports and the perspectives of foreign officials cannot be generalized beyond the seaports and officials visited because statistical sampling was not used. It also states that it is unclear who will pay for additional resources needed for 100 percent scanning; that mutual recognition is not easily or quickly attained and that adoption of the SAFE Framework does not by itself provide confidence in another country's customs security practices; that a WCO Private Sector Consultative Group official said more clarity is needed between the two types of mutual recognition; that hurdles such as verification of inspection and targeting programs remain before CBP personnel could be removed from European seaports; and that specific details of how mutual recognition arrangements will be implemented are still being worked out.

audience.name: Who it is for
audience.text: The report is addressed to the congressional requesters—the Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee; the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee and its Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations; and the House Committee on Energy and Commerce—to support their oversight of CBP's international supply chain security efforts and the 100 percent scanning requirement.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This document is a U.S. Government Accountability Office report, GAO-08-598, issued June 19, 2008, to the Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations of the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs. It assesses the progress the Nuclear Regulatory Commission has made in implementing recommendations from GAO's August 2003 report on radioactive sealed source security, other steps NRC has taken to monitor and track radioactive materials, Customs and Border Protection's ability to detect radioactive materials at northern and southern land ports of entry, and CBP's ability to verify that such materials are appropriately licensed before entering the United States.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: NRC has implemented three of the six recommendations from GAO's 2003 report, including identifying 16 radionuclides of concern, establishing increased controls for category 2 or greater quantities, and creating performance criteria for assessing implementation. NRC has made limited progress on modifying its licensing process, mitigating the psychological effects of an RDD, and re-examining whether certain sources should be regulated through specific rather than general licenses. NRC has taken four steps to improve monitoring and tracking, but three are delayed or limited; the National Source Tracking System has been delayed by 18 months and is not expected to launch until January 2009, and the Web-based licensing system is more than 3 years behind schedule. CBP has a comprehensive radiation detection system at land borders, but personal radiation detectors are in short supply, with about 1,500 needed for current officers and no current funding for about 2,000 more for new officers. CBP's May 2006 guidance requiring officers to contact the National Targeting Center to verify licenses when more than incidental, trace amounts of radiation are detected was not effectively communicated, and some dangerous radioactive materials, including neutron-emitting materials, entered the country without license verification.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: The report states that about 2 million sealed sources are licensed for use in the United States, and that of the approximately 22,000 specific materials licenses, NRC administers about 3,750 and agreement states administer the rest, with NRC having relinquished authority to 35 states. Under IAEA's system, a category 1 quantity is defined as an amount 1,000 times or more than the amount necessary to cause permanent human injury, a category 2 quantity as at least 10 times but less than 1,000 times that amount, and a category 3 quantity as at least the minimum amount but less than 10 times that amount. The 16 radionuclides of concern have IAEA category 2 thresholds in curies as follows: americium-241, 16; americium-241/beryllium, 16; californium-252, 5.4; cesium-137, 27; cobalt-60, 8.1; curium-244, 14; gadolinium-153, 270; iridium-192, 22; plutonium-238, 16; plutonium-239/beryllium, 16; promethium-147, 11,000; radium-226, 11; selenium-75, 54; strontium-90 (yttrium-90), 270; thulium-170, 5,400; and ytterbium-169, 81. NRC and agreement state regulators have already performed preliminary increased controls inspections on approximately 1,100 of the 1,700 licensees subject to the new controls, and 22 of the 35 agreement states and one of the three NRC regional offices have had aspects of their implementation at least partially assessed. The interim database includes information from 99 percent of all licensees. The National Source Tracking System will initially track category 1 and 2 sources of 20 radionuclides, which include the 16 radionuclides of concern plus actinium-227, polonium-210, and thorium-228 and -229. According to CBP, over 90 percent of personally owned vehicles entering the United States at land ports of entry pass through radiation portal monitors. CBP lacks sufficient resources to purchase the approximately 1,500 personal radiation detectors it needs for current officers, and has no money currently in the budget to acquire the approximately 2,000 additional detectors for new officers, leaving a shortfall of about 3,500. The NSTS launch is estimated for January 31, 2009, its expansion is estimated for March 2010, the Web-based licensing system is estimated to be completed no earlier than late summer 2010, and any rule change on general versus specific licenses may not be fully implemented until the fall of 2012.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The report recommends that the Chairman of the NRC take steps, consistent with sound systems development practices, to ensure that priority attention is given to meeting the current January 2009 and summer 2010 target dates for launching the National Source Tracking System, Web-based licensing system, and the new license verification system, respectively, and to complete the steps needed to include all potentially dangerous radioactive sources, namely category 3 and the larger category 4 sources as well as categories 1 and 2, in the National Source Tracking System as quickly as reasonably possible. The report also recommends that the Secretary of Homeland Security direct the Commissioner of Customs and Border Protection to effectively communicate current CBP guidance to officers at ports of entry regarding when they are required to contact the National Targeting Center to verify that radioactive materials are legitimately licensed, and to take measures to ensure that this guidance is being followed. In its conclusions, the report also states that NRC should correct the vulnerabilities uncovered in its materials licensing process, determine whether certain radioactive sources should be regulated through specific licenses rather than general licenses, and work with DHS, other federal agencies, and agreement states to develop a plan to effectively mitigate the potential psychological effects of an RDD event.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The report does not settle whether NRC's licensing process weaknesses have been fully corrected; it says it is too early to evaluate whether NRC's announced steps will be successful. It states that NRC has not yet determined how to effectively mitigate the potential psychological effects of an RDD, and that NRC has not yet decided whether certain radioactive sources should be regulated through specific licenses rather than general licenses. The report notes that the National Source Tracking System launch has been delayed multiple times and that past delays give reason to wonder whether the current dates will again be extended, and that the Web-based licensing system may not initially include information on agreement state licenses, which represent over 80 percent of all U.S. licenses for these materials. It also notes that CBP lacks sufficient resources for personal radiation detectors, that the updated directive incorporating the May 2006 memorandum had not been issued as of the report, and that NRC neither agreed nor disagreed with the report's findings and recommendations.

audience.name: Who it is for
audience.text: The intended audience is the Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations of the U.S. Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs, which requested the report for congressional oversight of nuclear security and radioactive materials tracking and detection.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This document is a July 25, 2008, U.S. Government Accountability Office report to congressional committees on federal payroll tax compliance. It covers the magnitude of unpaid federal payroll tax debt, the factors affecting the Internal Revenue Service's ability to enforce compliance and pursue collections against businesses with unpaid payroll taxes, and whether some businesses with unpaid payroll taxes are engaged in abusive or potentially criminal activities related to the federal tax system.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: GAO's analysis of IRS records as of September 30, 2007, found that over 1.6 million businesses owed over $58 billion in unpaid payroll taxes, including interest and penalties; 70 percent of that debt was owed by businesses with more than a year (4 tax quarters) of unpaid payroll taxes and over a quarter by businesses with more than 3 years (12 tax quarters). GAO found that IRS's collection approach focuses primarily on voluntary compliance, which can allow egregious payroll tax offenders to continue accumulating debt for years. IRS was not timely filing liens: over a third of businesses with unpaid payroll taxes assigned to the field had no lien filed, over 80 percent of payroll cases in the queue had no lien filed, and 60 percent of all unpaid payroll tax cases in IRS's inventory had no lien. IRS was not timely assessing Trust Fund Recovery Penalties: in a sample of 76 TFRP assessments, it took IRS over 40 weeks on average to decide to pursue collection against responsible owners or officers and an additional 40 weeks to assess the penalty, and half of the sampled TFRP assessments had not been assigned to a revenue officer by the time of the audit. GAO also found IRS did not prioritize collection against responsible owners or officers as highly as collection against the business and had no performance measures establishing goals for collection and prevention of unpaid payroll taxes. Case studies of 50 businesses showed owners and officers willfully diverting withheld payroll taxes to fund business operations or personal lifestyles, including underreporting personal income, possible check kiting and money laundering, large cash withdrawals before bankruptcy filings, and transferring property to family members to avoid IRS collection.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: IRS taxpayer service and enforcement efforts generate 96 percent of federal revenue; in 2007 IRS processed over 230 million tax returns and collected over $2.7 trillion in taxes, while enforcement programs collected over $40 billion. IRS estimated the annual net tax gap at nearly $300 billion. As of September 30, 2007, IRS records showed about $282 billion in outstanding taxes owed by businesses and individuals; over $58 billion (over 20 percent) was unpaid payroll taxes, owed by over 1.6 million businesses. Payroll taxes were $58 billion (53 percent) of business taxes owed; corporate income taxes $24 billion (22 percent); estate $6 billion (6 percent); unemployment $4 billion (4 percent); excise $3 billion (3 percent); other $13 billion (12 percent). Of the payroll tax debt, $18 billion (30 percent) was 1 to 4 quarters outstanding, $15 billion (25 percent) 5 to 8 quarters, $10 billion (17 percent) 9 to 12 quarters, $10 billion (18 percent) 13 to 20 quarters, $5 billion (9 percent) 21 to 40 quarters, and less than $1 billion (1 percent) more than 40 quarters. By tax year, $6 billion (10 percent) was prior to 1997, $29 billion (51 percent) 1997 to 2002, $21 billion (35 percent) 2003 to 2006, and $2 billion (4 percent) tax year 2007. The debt comprised $26 billion (46 percent) taxes, $18 billion (30 percent) interest, and $14 billion (24 percent) penalties. By collection status, $30 billion (52 percent) was currently not collectible, $9 billion (16 percent) in queue, $7 billion (12 percent) in field collections, $4 billion (7 percent) in notice, $2 billion (3 percent) bankruptcy or litigation, and $6 billion (10 percent) other. Of currently not collectible debt, $20 billion (66 percent) was from defunct businesses, $4 billion (13 percent) insolvent post-bankruptcy, $2 billion (7 percent) hardship, $2 billion (7 percent) in-business, and $2 billion (7 percent) other. IRS estimated the General Fund had transferred $44 billion to the Social Security and Hospital Insurance trust funds over what IRS collected for the unpaid assessments on record as of November 1, 2007, and recent IRS data indicate a shortfall of about $2 billion to $4 billion annually. From 1998 to September 30, 2007, the number of businesses with payroll tax debt decreased from 1.8 million to 1.6 million while the balance increased from about $49 billion to $58 billion; businesses with over 20 quarters of debt rose from 5,367 to 14,681 (174 percent), and those with over 40 quarters rose from 86 to 490 (470 percent). In 2007, FICA taxes to be withheld consisted of 6.2 percent of an employee's gross salary up to $97,500 for Social Security taxes and 1.45 percent for hospital insurance. IRS reported filing more than 680,000 tax liens in fiscal year 2007, over 3.7 million levy actions, and 676 seizure actions, compared with over 10,000 seizure actions in 1997. In fiscal year 2007 IRS collected over $17 billion from almost 3 million tax debtors through installment agreements. The 2005 IRS TFRP study reported over $11.9 billion in TFRP assessments between 1996 and 2004, with only 8 percent collected; 43 percent of assessed individuals never made a payment. IRS found over 1,500 individuals responsible for non-payment of payroll taxes at 3 or more businesses and 18 responsible for not remitting payroll taxes for 12 different businesses. IRS's inventory showed over $4 billion of unpaid payroll taxes will expire in each of the next several years; expirations by year were $4.2 billion in 2008, $4.3 billion in 2009, $4.2 billion in 2010, $4.6 billion in 2011, $5.1 billion in 2012, $4.7 billion in 2013, $4.6 billion in 2014, $5.1 billion in 2015, and $5.9 billion in 2016.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: GAO makes six recommendations to the Commissioner of IRS. Five are for IRS to review or revise its collection policies to provide better monitoring or more detailed guidance on collection actions to be taken against egregious payroll tax offenders and to strengthen its existing collection tools. The sixth is for IRS to work with states to develop ways of more effectively identifying potential levy sources. IRS concurred with all six recommendations and agreed to evaluate existing practices and determine appropriate changes, and to work with states matching financial institution accounts to tax debt to determine whether a similar program in IRS would be cost effective and consistent with privacy laws.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The report states that its figures understate the true cumulative amount of unpaid taxes because IRS has a statutory limitation, generally 10 years, on collection and removes tax debt after that period, and because many tax debts go unidentified and unrecorded due to non-filing or underreporting. The $44 billion estimate of General Fund transfers is a snapshot of outstanding debt on IRS's books as of November 1, 2007, and does not include tax debts written off in previous years due to expiration of the statutory collection period. GAO did not attempt to identify how frequently IRS assesses a TFRP against responsible owners or officers, and was unable to determine how many of the fewer than 700 fiscal year 2007 seizure actions were taken against payroll tax debtors. The report also notes that circumstances may not warrant a lien being filed in all cases, such as when businesses are highly leveraged or have few tangible assets, and leaves open whether an IRS program to identify levy sources through financial institution account matching would be cost effective and consistent with privacy laws.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This is a U.S. Government Accountability Office report (GAO-08-641), issued May 30, 2008, on the Department of Energy's Office of Science. It reports on the extent to which Science managed its projects within committed cost and schedule targets from fiscal year 2003 through fiscal year 2007, the key factors affecting that performance, and the main future challenges, particularly funding uncertainties and the shrinking pool of experienced staff. The report covers 42 projects at 10 national laboratories, with a detailed review of 12 of those projects.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: GAO found that more than two-thirds of the 42 Science projects completed or under way from fiscal year 2003 through fiscal year 2007 stayed within their original cost and schedule targets. Of the 27 completed projects, 24 (89 percent) met original cost targets and 21 (78 percent) were completed on or ahead of schedule; 2 (7 percent) were both over budget and late. Of the 15 projects still under way as of the end of February 2008, 9 (60 percent) were on track to meet both targets, 4 (27 percent) were expected to meet cost but not schedule, and 2 (13 percent) were expected to miss both. The successful performance is attributed to leadership commitment, management and technical expertise, disciplined and rigorous project oversight, and occasional trimming of project scope. Future challenges identified are heightened funding and market uncertainties and a shrinking pool of qualified staff as retirements increase.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: The Office of Science has a $4 billion annual budget and works through 10 national laboratories and 42 research and development facilities. GAO reviewed 42 projects from fiscal year 2003 through fiscal year 2007: 27 completed and 15 under way as of the end of February 2008. Of the completed projects, 24 (89 percent) met cost targets and 21 (78 percent) met schedule targets; 2 (7 percent) were both over cost and late, finishing 18 percent and 23 percent over cost and over 1 year late. Of the 15 under way, 9 (60 percent) were on track to meet cost and schedule, 4 (27 percent) to meet cost only, and 2 (13 percent) to miss both. GAO selected 12 projects for in-depth review, representing about $2.9 billion, or 75 percent, of the total value of the 42 projects. Science's independent review panels had up to 30 experts, and some projects received as many as 17 reviews. The Run IIb CDF Detector was completed for around $10.9 million, 64 percent less than the $30.4 million target, and 4 months ahead of schedule; the Run IIb D-Zero Detector was completed 39 percent below its original $29 million target. The Center for Nanoscale Materials at Argonne was completed on schedule within its $72 million target, with $36 million of specialized instruments and an 88,000-square-foot facility. An Oak Ridge HVAC upgrade was finished 4 months early for about $150,000 less than the $7.2 million target. Two Oak Ridge and Argonne projects each cost $5.9 million, finishing respectively about 3 months and about 15 months late. The Neutrinos at the Main Injector project cost $168 million, took 72 months, and was completed 17 months late at more than 23 percent over committed cost. The SPEAR 3 Upgrade was completed in 2003 for $58 million, 14 months late and nearly 18 percent over its original $49 million target. The National Compact Stellarator Experiment was projected to increase cost by 91 percent and delay completion by 4.5 years. The Large Area Telescope project increased from $121 million to $188 million, with DOE's direct contribution rising from $37 million to $45 million. A safety and operational reliability improvement project at Stanford was $15.7 million. Fiscal year 2008 funding for the U.S. contribution to the International Thermonuclear Experimental Reactor was $10.7 million rather than the $160 million requested. About 21 percent of Science's workforce was eligible for retirement in 2005, expected to rise to 43 percent by 2011, and Science staffing had declined by almost 15 percent since 1999. About 23,000 people work on Science projects at contractor laboratories. Science and engineering occupations grew at an average annual rate of 3.6 percent between 1990 and 2000.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: GAO recommends that the Secretary of Energy direct the Director of the Office of Engineering and Construction Management to consider whether other DOE program offices would benefit from adopting selected practices from Science's independent project reviews, such as the frequency and focus of reviews for technically complex projects. GAO also recommends that the Secretary of Energy direct the Office of Engineering and Construction Management to review DOE's project management guidance and consider whether it could be strengthened to help ensure that each project's technical goals, including expected scientific performance and corresponding facility requirements, are clearly and sufficiently defined. DOE generally agreed with the findings and stated it would consider incorporating the recommendations into its Root Cause Analysis: Corrective Action Plan.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The report does not settle whether scope reductions on the Spallation Neutron Source compromised the project's technical goals; the DOE Inspector General and the Office of Science disagreed, in part because the technical goals were broadly defined. It notes that the 12-project in-depth sample was nongeneralizable and cannot be used to make inferences about Science's overall performance, and that GAO did not consider DOE's Project Assessment Reporting System fully reliable. The report also notes that DOE officials were considering clarifying project management guidance on defining technical goals, perhaps by 2009, and that contractor laboratories had not yet estimated the shortfall in project management and scientific expertise from future retirements. The future effects of federal fiscal constraints and volatile market prices are presented as uncertainties rather than settled outcomes.

audience.text: This report is addressed to the Chairman and Ranking Member of the Subcommittee on Investigations and Oversight, Committee on Science and Technology, House of Representatives, to support congressional oversight, policy, and funding decisions.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This GAO report, GAO-08-684, issued June 13, 2008, examines the status of 30 property conveyances and transfers between the District of Columbia and the federal government directed by Public Law 109-396, the steps taken and remaining to complete them, preliminary development and current plans, and the development challenges ahead, as part of a 10-year periodic reporting mandate.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: GAO found that no property conveyances between the District and the federal government had occurred as of June 6, 2008, although all transfers of administrative jurisdiction became effective on December 15, 2006. The District and federal government had taken several steps toward completing the conveyances, including forming working groups and executing a District-GSA exchange agreement, but cleanup negotiations, contamination testing, disagreement over Boathouse Row land, and the need to agree on a property for the Architect of the Capitol slowed progress. Limited development had occurred on the exchanged properties, and development will take many years. Poplar Point and Reservation 13 are the largest conveyed properties and are expected to generate most of the new tax revenue to reduce the District's structural fiscal imbalance, but development of Poplar Point is not likely to begin until 2011 and may take up to a decade, and Reservation 13 construction may also take as long as a decade. The District and federal government face challenges including cleanup and development uncertainties at Poplar Point, the transition of the Deputy Mayor's office into a development coordination role, and reaching community agreement about development.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: The document reports that no property conveyances had occurred as of June 6, 2008; all transfers of administrative jurisdiction became effective December 15, 2006. Poplar Point is a 110-acre property and Reservation 13 is a 67-acre property. The Master Developer's vision for Poplar Point includes 1.5 million square feet of office space, 3.8 million square feet of residential units, 405,000 square feet of retail space, 70 acres of parks, a waterfront entertainment district, a deck over I-295, and an option for a soccer stadium. At least 51 percent of the new jobs created at Poplar Point must go to District residents, and 35 percent of contracting dollars must be awarded to small and local businesses. For Reservation 13, the site can accommodate about 3,000 new housing units, nearly 5.5 million square feet of mixed-use development, new public park spaces, and more than $80 million in new infrastructure upgrades. Current NPS and USPP facilities at Poplar Point encompass 100,000 square feet, sit on approximately 18 acres, and include a 5-acre helicopter landing area requirement and a 10-acre safety zone requirement. Relocation of NPS and USPP facilities will likely take 18 to 24 months, and meeting NEPA requirements will likely take 12 to 15 months. The District's structural fiscal imbalance likely exceeded $470 million annually and could have been as high as $1.1 billion, with per capita service costs approximately 75 percent, or $2.3 billion more annually, above the average state fiscal system. DMPED staff increased from 33 full-time equivalents in September 2007 to 63 in June 2008 and was expected to grow to 73 by August 2008. The Architect of the Capitol is to receive not more than 12 acres of District property for an offsite delivery facility. The five St. Elizabeths buildings to be conveyed to GSA total 6.55 acres. Reservation 174 is a 0.25-acre property whose conveyance is conditioned on a plan setting aside no fewer than 1.25 acres of the former Convention Center Site as open space.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: This document makes no recommendations.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The document does not settle the extent and location of cleanup required at Poplar Point, the cost of environmental cleanup, who will pay for it, the potential complications of relocating U.S. Park Police facilities, or how much construction may occur before the NPS Director certifies replacement facilities are ready. It notes that the meaning of 'construction project' under the statute was unclear and that NPS lawyers were examining it. It also notes uncertainty about whether the Deputy Mayor's office can effectively manage the many development projects and whether community agreement can be reached about development at Poplar Point. The AOC expressed concern that it had not received supporting instruments of transfer, including surveys and legal descriptions, from the District. The report also states that estimates of the structural imbalance could change if the underlying assumptions change.

audience.name: Who it is for
audience.text: It is addressed to the congressional committees specified in the mandate: the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee and the House Oversight and Government Reform, Energy and Commerce, Natural Resources, and Transportation and Infrastructure Committees.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This document is a U.S. Government Accountability Office report to the Ranking Member of the Subcommittee on Oversight and Investigations, Committee on Energy and Commerce, House of Representatives, issued August 8, 2008. It examines, for 2006, the extent to which medically underserved areas (MUAs) lacked health center sites and the services each site provided; how new access point grants awarded in 2007 changed the extent to which MUAs lacked sites; and HRSA's oversight of cooperative agreement recipients that assist new access point applicants and the feedback HRSA gives unsuccessful applicants.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: GAO found that in 2006, 47 percent of MUAs nationwide lacked a health center site, with wide variation by census region and state, and that the types of services provided at individual health center sites could not be determined because HRSA does not collect and maintain readily available site-level data. GAO found that new access point grants awarded in 2007 reduced the number of MUAs lacking a site by about 7 percent, leaving 43 percent lacking a site in 2007, but wide geographic variation remained, with most of the decline concentrated in the South. GAO found that HRSA oversees cooperative agreement recipients through regular communications, review of applications, and comprehensive on-site reviews, but oversight is limited because HRSA lacks standardized performance measures and is unlikely to meet its 3-to-5-year on-site review timeline. GAO also found that 38 percent of summary statements sent to unsuccessful applicants for fiscal years 2005 and 2007 new access point competitions contained unclear feedback.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: In 2006, approximately 1,000 health center grantees operated more than 6,000 health center sites while serving more than 15 million people, and Health Center Program grants made up about 20 percent of grantees' revenues. For fiscal year 2007, HRSA awarded nearly $53 million in training and technical assistance cooperative agreements. In 2006, 47 percent of MUAs nationwide—1,600 of 3,421—lacked a health center site; by census region, 62 percent of MUAs in the Midwest, 45 percent in the South, 39 percent in the Northeast, and 32 percent in the West lacked a site. Including 294 health center look-alike sites in 2006, 46 percent of MUAs (1,564) lacked a health center site or look-alike site. In 2007, new access point awards left 1,487 MUAs lacking a site, 113 fewer than in 2006, or 43 percent. By census region in 2007, the percentages lacking a site were 37 percent in the Northeast, 40 percent in the South, 60 percent in the Midwest, and 31 percent in the West; with 265 look-alike sites included, 1,462 MUAs lacked a site or look-alike site, still 43 percent. The 2006-to-2007 decreases were 6 MUAs (4 percent) in the Northeast, 24 (4 percent) in the Midwest, 77 (12 percent) in the South, 6 (4 percent) in the West, and 113 (7 percent) nationally. In 2007, 202 new access point grants were awarded: 39 (19 percent) in the Midwest, 15 (7 percent) in the Northeast, 101 (50 percent) in the South, and 47 (23 percent) in the West. In the High Poverty County competition, 69 percent of awards went to the South, and nearly two-thirds of the 200 targeted counties were in the South. In the open competition, 127 grants were awarded: 21 (17 percent) in the Midwest, 12 (9 percent) in the Northeast, 49 (39 percent) in the South, and 45 (35 percent) in the West. HRSA has conducted comprehensive on-site reviews for fewer than one-quarter (about 20 percent) of training and technical assistance cooperative agreement recipients that target assistance to new access point applicants since 2004. Of 230 summary statements sent to unsuccessful applicants in fiscal years 2005 and 2007, GAO sampled 69; 38 percent contained unclear feedback, 13 percent contained unclear feedback in more than one criterion, and 26 statements contained unclear feedback, with 41 distinct examples. The distinct examples by criterion were: need 11, response 7, impact 5, support requested 5, evaluative measures 4, governance 4, readiness 3, and resources/capabilities 2. In 2006, 32 percent of MUAs contained more than one health center site; among MUAs with at least one site, 60 percent contained multiple sites. States where three-quarters or more of MUAs contained more than one site were Alaska, Connecticut, the District of Columbia, Hawaii, New Hampshire, and Rhode Island; Nebraska, Iowa, and North Dakota had less than 10 percent of MUAs with multiple sites. More than three-quarters of MUAs in Nebraska (91 percent), Iowa (82 percent), Minnesota (77 percent), and Montana (77 percent) lacked a site, while fewer than one-quarter in Colorado (21 percent), California (20 percent), Mississippi (20 percent), and West Virginia (19 percent) lacked a site. Of 387 applications submitted for fiscal year 2007 new access point competitions, 363 were eligible. For new access point grant applications, the 2005 and 2007 open competitions awarded up to 100 total points: need 10, response 30, evaluative measures 10, impact 10, resources/capabilities 15, support requested 10, governance 10, and readiness 5. The 2007 high poverty county competition also totaled 100 points: need 35, response 20, evaluative measures 5, impact 6, resources/capabilities 11, support requested 8, governance 10, and readiness 5.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The report recommends that the Administrator of HRSA take four actions: collect and maintain readily available data on the types of services provided at each health center site; develop and implement standardized performance measures for training and technical assistance cooperative agreement recipients, including a measure of the number of successful grant applicants a recipient assisted; reevaluate the policy of requiring comprehensive on-site reviews of training and technical assistance cooperative agreement recipients every 3 to 5 years and consider targeting available resources at recipients that would benefit most; and identify and take appropriate action to ensure that the discussion of applicants' strengths and weaknesses in all summary statements is clear. The report states that HHS concurred with the second, third, and fourth recommendations and raised concerns about the first.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The report states that it could not determine the types of services provided at individual health center sites in MUAs because HRSA does not collect and maintain readily available site-level data, and therefore the extent to which individuals in MUAs have access to the full range of comprehensive primary care services is unknown. It also states that HRSA officials provided no details on the specific standardized performance measures they may implement, so it is unclear to what extent the proposed measures will allow HRSA to assess recipients' performance. The report notes that, without comprehensive on-site reviews, HRSA does not have a means of obtaining comprehensive information on the performance of cooperative agreement recipients. It also notes that the summary-statement analysis used a random sample of 69 of 230 statements and is generalizable to that universe. With respect to HHS's comments, GAO acknowledges that it did not include MUPs in the analysis, did not explicitly account for the proximity of sites located outside an MUA, and did not examine whether MUAs were sufficiently served; GAO responds that MUPs were beyond the scope, its zip-code-based method may overestimate the number of MUAs containing a site, and site-level service data were not available. The report also notes an assumption that all health center sites operating in 2006 were still operating in 2007 because UDS data had not been updated, and records HHS's position that collecting site-specific service information would place a significant burden on grantees and raise administrative expenses.

audience.text: The report is addressed to the Ranking Member of the Subcommittee on Oversight and Investigations, Committee on Energy and Commerce, House of Representatives, and is intended to support congressional oversight of the Health Resources and Services Administration's Health Center Program.
