about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This document is a U.S. Government Accountability Office report to congressional committees, GAO-08-732, released June 10, 2008. It examines U.S. assistance provided to the Republic of Palau under the Compact of Free Association and related programs from 1995 through 2009, Palau's and U.S. agencies' accountability for the use of federal funds in 1995-2006, and Palau's prospects for economic self-sufficiency. It also reviews amendments made to the U.S. compacts with the Federated States of Micronesia and the Republic of the Marshall Islands and their relevance to Palau's compact review.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The report finds that U.S. assistance to Palau in 1995-2009—compact direct assistance, compact federal services, compact road construction, and discretionary federal programs—is expected to exceed $852 million. Compact direct assistance accounts for $411 million, or 48 percent; discretionary federal programs for about $267 million, or 31 percent; compact road construction for $149 million, or 17 percent; and compact federal services for about $25 million, or 3 percent. Palau made progress in financial accountability—improving timeliness of single audit submissions and reliability of financial statements—but has limited capacity to address persistent internal control weaknesses, and Interior's oversight has been limited. Palau's prospects for economic self-sufficiency depend on four factors: levels of continued U.S. assistance, the availability and value of trust fund withdrawals, fiscal reform, and private sector growth. A compounded annual return of at least 8.1 percent would allow Palau to withdraw $15 million per year from the trust fund for 35 years; the fund earned 9 percent from 1995 through March 2008, but market volatility makes depletion possible after 2016, and the probability of depletion reaches approximately 46 percent by 2044.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: The report projects total U.S. assistance to Palau for 1995-2009 at more than $852 million: $411 million in compact direct assistance (48 percent), $266.7 million in discretionary federal programs (31 percent), $149 million for the compact road (17 percent), and $25.3 million in compact federal services (3 percent). Compact direct assistance includes $120 million under section 211(a), $28 million under 211(b), $3.75 million under 211(c), $9.5 million under 211(d), $0.7 million under 211(e), $70 million under 211(f), $36 million under 212(b), $5.5 million under 213, $98.9 million in inflation adjustments under 215, and $38.7 million in special block grants under 221(b) and the federal programs and services agreement. Federal services are estimated at $12.3 million for USPS, $8.6 million for NWS, and $4.4 million for FAA. In 1995-2006, five agencies contributed the majority of discretionary assistance: Education $56.2 million, HHS $51.6 million, Interior $39.1 million, DOD $23.8 million, DOT $12.9 million, with other agencies $19.8 million. For 2009, Palau's potential revenues are estimated at $86.6 million: domestic revenue $43.6 million, other donor assistance $17.8 million, discretionary federal programs $11.9 million, and compact direct assistance $13.3 million. Expiring compact direct assistance would have a net fiscal impact of about $3.3 million a year, or less than 4 percent of 2009 revenues. Compact federal services in 2009 are estimated to cost U.S. agencies almost $1.6 million. The Palau trust fund had a balance of $160.775 million as of March 2008. A compounded annual return of at least 8.1 percent would sustain $15 million annual withdrawals for 35 years; 8.6 percent would let the fund grow in perpetuity; the fund earned 9 percent from inception through March 2008. Historical compounded returns for the fund's asset classes were 8.1 percent for 1926-2007, 9.1 percent for 1970-2007, and 5.2 percent for 1998-2007. Annual trust fund returns ranged from 24 percent in 1998 to negative 12 percent in 2002. By 2030 the probability of depletion is close to 26 percent, and by 2044 approximately 46 percent. In 2006 Palau's GDP was about $154 million, GDP per capita about $7,500, national government expenditures $89 million, and U.S. and other donor grants $44 million. The national government wage bill averaged 40 percent of total expenditures from 2000 to 2006.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The report recommends that the Secretary of the Interior direct the Office of Insular Affairs to (1) formally consult with the government of Palau regarding Palau's financial management challenges and (2) target future technical assistance toward building Palau's financial management capacity. The Department of the Interior agreed with the report and recommendation and said it had begun making plans to implement the recommendation; the government of Palau also agreed. The Department of State did not comment. The compact also requires the U.S. and Palau governments to review the terms of the compact in 2009 and to make any modifications by mutual agreement, and it requires Palau to submit annual single audit reports, economic development plans every 5 years, and annual reports.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The report does not settle whether Palau will achieve economic self-sufficiency: it says prospects depend on multiple factors and are subject to considerable uncertainty. Future trust fund returns are uncertain; market volatility makes depletion possible after 2016 even with a favorable long-term average return, and inflation will cut the real value of the fixed $15 million withdrawals by about half by 2044. Future levels of discretionary federal programs are uncertain because they depend on Palau's eligibility and congressional appropriations, and U.S. agency officials were uncertain about the impact of the expiration of the federal programs and services agreement. The report says Palau has limited capacity to execute corrective action plans in a timely way, putting at risk the sustainability of its financial accountability improvements. It also states that required annual economic consultations were not held annually and trust fund consultations did not take place, and that lack of documentation prevents assessment of the consultations' effectiveness. It notes concerns about Palau's ability to maintain the compact road in a condition that will allow desired economic development.

audience.name: Who it is for
audience.text: The audience is the U.S. Congress—specifically the Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources and the House Subcommittee on Insular Affairs—to support the mandated 2009 review of the Compact of Free Association with Palau.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This is a June 2008 U.S. Government Accountability Office report, GAO-08-741, addressed to the Ranking Member of the Subcommittee on Economic Opportunity, Committee on Veterans' Affairs, House of Representatives. It compares the amount of Title IV federal student aid awarded to veteran students with that awarded to nonveteran, independent students, examines how higher education institutions allocate Title IV aid among veteran and nonveteran students, and examines how federal agencies and schools provide information to veterans about Title IV aid. The scope covers veterans and active-duty personnel who served for 3 or more years and received Montgomery GI Bill Chapter 30 benefits, and it uses 2005 to 2006 Education data for Pell Grants and Stafford Loans, 2003 to 2004 data for campus-based aid, and 2005 to 2006 Chapter 30 GI benefit amounts.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The report's main findings are that veteran students overall received similar amounts of Title IV aid as nonveteran, independent students, but when Chapter 30 GI benefits were included, veterans received more total federal aid than nonveterans. Laws and regulations largely dictate how schools allocate Title IV aid among veteran and nonveteran students, but five of the eight schools interviewed used their limited flexibility to allow veterans to be eligible for larger amounts of certain types of Title IV aid. Federal agencies and schools provide the same Title IV information to all students, but two of the eight schools reached out to veteran students at nearby military bases, and in 2007 Education began new efforts such as workshops on federal aid for personnel separating from the military. Veterans received, on average, 6 percent less in Pell Grants than nonveterans, which the report attributes to veterans' higher incomes rather than to Chapter 30 GI benefits, and veterans received similar amounts of subsidized and unsubsidized Stafford Loans and campus-based aid as nonveterans. The report also finds that Chapter 30 GI benefits are not counted as income in expected family contribution and are excluded from estimated financial assistance in determining eligibility for subsidized Stafford Loans, which can make veterans eligible for larger subsidized loans than nonveterans receiving comparable scholarships.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: The report states that in fiscal year 2007 the Department of Education provided $82 billion in Title IV grants, loans, and work-study aid to 11 million students and their families, and VA awarded about $2 billion in Chapter 30 Montgomery GI Bill benefits to more than 300,000 veteran students. Over the past decade, average college tuition and fees increased between 20 and 38 percent, depending on the type of institution. For academic year 2005 to 2006, average aid amounts for first-year, full-time students were: Pell Grants $2,322 for veterans and $2,482 for nonveteran independent students; subsidized Stafford Loans $2,082 for veterans and $2,109 for nonveterans; unsubsidized Stafford Loans $2,959 for veterans and $2,945 for nonveterans; campus-based aid in 2003 to 2004 was $1,450 for veterans and $1,300 for nonveterans, estimates that were not significantly different at the 95 percent confidence level; and Chapter 30 GI benefits were $9,306 for veterans. Chapter 30 GI benefit recipients who completed three or more years of active-duty service and attended college full-time received $1,034 per month for a maximum of 36 months, and servicemembers contribute $100 per month for the first 12 months of service. Program award ranges cited for award year 2005 to 2006 include Pell Grants of $400 to $4,050 (and $400 to $4,310 for 2007 to 2008), subsidized Stafford Loans up to $2,625 (up to $3,500 for 2007 to 2008), and unsubsidized Stafford Loans up to $6,625 for independent undergraduates (up to $7,500 for 2007 to 2008); FSEOG awards were $100 to $4,000, except up to $4,400 for study-abroad, Perkins Loans up to $4,000, and Federal Work-Study had no annual minimum or maximum award amount. At the 75th income percentile at public 2-year schools in 2005 to 2006, veterans earned $38,550 the year before starting school and were eligible for a Pell Grant of $1,600, compared with $33,259 and $2,100 for nonveterans. about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This GAO report (GAO-08-825, issued September 2008) examines the Department of Homeland Security's first Cyber Storm exercise: it identifies the eight lessons DHS learned from Cyber Storm I, assesses DHS's progress in addressing those lessons through corrective activities, and reports key participants' observations of progress and continued challenges during Cyber Storm II. It concludes with one recommendation for executive action before the next Cyber Storm exercise, which was planned for 2010.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The report's findings are GAO's own, based on its review of DHS documents, interviews with DHS officials and exercise participants, and attendance at Cyber Storm II. DHS identified eight lessons from Cyber Storm I, covering interagency coordination groups; contingency planning, risk assessment, and roles and responsibilities; integration of incidents across infrastructures; access to information; coordination of response activities; strategic communications and public relations; processes, tools, and technology; and the exercise program. DHS identified 66 activities to address these lessons and had completed 42 of them, with 1 reported as completed but not validated, 16 ongoing, and 7 planned for the future. The report finds that key activities remained incomplete, that DHS had not set completion dates for ongoing activities, and that DHS therefore risked repeating the first exercise's lessons in subsequent exercises. Cyber Storm II participants observed both progress and continued challenges, and many of the challenges were similar to those identified in Cyber Storm I.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: Cyber Storm I was conducted in February 2006 at a cost of about $3.7 million and involved eight federal departments and three agencies, three states, four foreign countries, 11 information technology companies, 7 electric companies, 1 banking and finance company, 2 airlines, and over 100 public and private agencies, associations, and corporations. Cyber Storm II was conducted in March 2008 at a cost of about $6.4 million and, according to DHS, involved 18 federal agencies, 9 states, 10 information sharing and analysis centers, 5 foreign countries, and over 40 industry representatives. DHS identified 66 activities to address the Cyber Storm I lessons; as of June 2008, 42 were reported and validated as completed, 1 was reported as completed but not validated due to insufficient evidence, 16 were reported as ongoing, and 7 were reported as planned for the future. DHS listed 121 activities to address lessons 1 through 8, but 55 of these repeat a prior activity. The report states DHS completed over 60 percent of these activities, and DHS reported raising the percentage to over 70 percent after receiving the draft report. By lesson, DHS identified 32 activities for interagency coordination groups, of which 24 were completed; 15 for contingency planning, risk assessment, and roles and responsibilities, of which 8 were completed; 16 for integration of incidents across infrastructures, of which 9 were completed; 15 for access to information, of which 8 were completed; 15 for coordination of response activities, of which 11 were completed; 5 for strategic communications and public relations, of which 1 was completed; 12 for processes, tools, and technology, of which 8 were completed; and 11 for the exercise program, of which 9 were completed.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The document makes one recommendation to the Secretary of Homeland Security: direct the Assistant Secretary for Cybersecurity and Communications to ensure the scheduling and completion of the corrective actions addressing lessons learned during Cyber Storm I before conducting the next Cyber Storm exercise. DHS concurred with the recommendation and reported that it will continue to address actions related to Cyber Storm I findings. The document also notes that federal policy and DHS exercise guidance require corrective-action tracking, but the sole recommendation for executive action is the one described here.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The document does not settle the completion of all corrective activities: DHS had not identified completion dates for the 16 activities reported as ongoing, and GAO could not validate one activity reported as completed because DHS was unable to provide evidence demonstrating its completion. After receiving the draft report, DHS reported completing additional items, but GAO did not modify the statuses because DHS had not yet provided sufficient evidence. DHS stated that end dates are not applicable for many remaining corrective actions because they are dependent on outside stakeholder actions or are ongoing or long-term, while GAO found that most of the remaining activities are finite and could be associated with a time frame. The report also states that observations from Cyber Storm II participants are not intended to be generalized to other exercise participants. DHS planned to issue a report on what it learned from Cyber Storm II by the end of 2008, and a third Cyber Storm exercise was planned for 2010, but the document does not settle the outcomes of those efforts.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This document is a June 27, 2008 U.S. Government Accountability Office report to congressional committees, mandated by the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2008, reviewing the Department of Homeland Security's risk-based grant allocation methodology for the Homeland Security Grant Program, specifically the State Homeland Security Program and the Urban Areas Security Initiative. It addresses how the methodology changed from fiscal year 2007 to fiscal year 2008 and how reasonable the fiscal year 2008 methodology is, with particular attention to the vulnerability element of DHS's risk analysis model.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: GAO found that DHS is primarily following the same three-step methodology in fiscal year 2008 as in fiscal year 2007—risk analysis, effectiveness assessment, and final allocation—with the principal change being the shift to Census Bureau metropolitan statistical areas to define UASI urban area footprints, reflecting the 9/11 Act requirement to assess the 100 largest MSAs. The change altered urban area footprints and relative risk rankings and led DHS to expand eligible urban areas to 60 UASI grantees. GAO concluded that DHS's methodology is generally reasonable because it includes threat, vulnerability, and consequences, uses generally reasonable consequence indices, and became less sensitive to changes in assumptions in fiscal year 2008, particularly for Tier 2 eligibility. However, GAO found that the vulnerability element is limited: DHS assigned every state and urban area a vulnerability score of 1.0, so final risk scores are determined by the threat and consequences scores, and differences in vulnerability across states and urban areas are ignored.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: Since 2002, DHS has distributed almost $20 billion in federal funding through various DHS grant programs. In fiscal year 2007, DHS provided approximately $1.7 billion to states and urban areas through the Homeland Security Grant Program, and planned to distribute approximately $1.6 billion in fiscal year 2008. DHS used the same risk-based methodology to allocate $852 million in fiscal year 2008 under the Infrastructure Protection Program, and used the same approach to allocate $655 million in fiscal year 2007 under that program. SHSP provides funding to all 56 states and territories. In fiscal year 2007, 45 urban areas were eligible for UASI funding: 6 Tier 1 areas received 55 percent of available funds, approximately $410.8 million, and 39 Tier 2 areas received 45 percent, approximately $336.1 million. In fiscal year 2008, 60 urban areas were eligible: 7 Tier 1 areas received 55 percent, approximately $429.9 million, and 53 Tier 2 areas received 45 percent, approximately $351.7 million. The maximum relative risk score was 100; the Threat Index accounted for 20 percent and the Vulnerability and Consequences Index for 80 percent. Within the Vulnerability and Consequences Index, the Population Index was 40 percent, the Economic Index 20 percent, the National Infrastructure Index 15 percent, and the National Security Index 5 percent. DHS assigned vulnerability a constant value of 1.0. The change to MSAs increased the total urban area footprint by almost 162,000 square miles; 3 urban areas lost square mileage and the other areas increased by almost 2,700 square miles on average. Tier 1 assets were weighted three times as much as Tier 2 assets, and the Tier 1 criteria include prompt fatalities greater than 5,000, first-year economic impact of at least $75 billion, mass evacuations with prolonged absence of 6 months or more, and loss of governance or mission execution for more than a week. The fiscal year 2008 statutory minimum was 0.375 percent of all funds appropriated for SHSP and UASI (0.008 percent for territories), decreasing to 0.35 percent by fiscal year 2012; in fiscal years 2006 and 2007 the statutory minimum was 0.75 percent.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The document recommends that the Secretary of DHS instruct FEMA, I&A, and NPPD—the DHS components responsible for aspects of the risk-based methodology used to allocate funds under the Homeland Security Grant Program—to formulate a method to measure vulnerability in a way that captures variations across states and urban areas, and apply this vulnerability measure in future iterations of the risk-based grant allocation model. The report notes that FEMA and I&A concurred with this recommendation.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The document does not settle how vulnerability should be measured across states and urban areas; it reports that DHS did not measure vulnerability in fiscal years 2007 and 2008 and assigned a constant value of 1.0, and that DHS previously noted it would require substantial time and resource investment to fully develop the capability to consistently assess and compare vulnerabilities across all types of infrastructure. It also reports inherent uncertainty in estimating the risk of terrorist attack, that DHS officials expressed limited confidence in the formula's ability to adequately represent threat, that DHS's analysis of the peer review process did not apply a generally accepted method to ensure inter-rater reliability, that DHS cited resource constraints as a reason for not measuring inter-rater reliability, and that DHS did not provide details on what criteria its 'best fit' footprint comparison was based on. It also notes that threat assessments were shared only with state officials who had appropriate security clearances, with an unclassified version planned for states without such officials for the fiscal year 2009 grant process, and that DHS was still developing a process to share the assessments with UASI areas.

audience.text: The audience is the congressional appropriations committees and their Subcommittees on Homeland Security in the U.S. Senate and House of Representatives, which oversee DHS's risk-based allocation of Homeland Security Grant Program funds.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This GAO report, GAO-08-854, issued June 26, 2008, examines the extent to which federal agencies use the authorities of the Defense Production Act of 1950 since the 2003 reauthorization, in the areas of defense, energy, domestic emergency and disaster response and recovery, and critical infrastructure protection and restoration, and assesses agencies' response to reporting requirements on the economic impact of foreign offsets.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The document finds that DOD is the primary user of DPA authorities, routinely placing priority ratings on almost all of its contracts for industrial resources, while civilian agencies have generally not used the Title I priority and allocations authority and most would apply it on a case-by-case basis after delivery issues are identified, potentially delaying delivery of critical products in emergencies. It finds that agencies responsible for civil transportation, health resources, and food and agriculture resources lack developed policies or guidance for using the authority; HHS and USDA are developing regulations and DOT has not begun. It also finds that Title III authority has been used almost exclusively for defense needs, that events have not triggered use of some Title VII authorities, and that efforts to assess foreign offsets have been limited by the type of data collected, by a lack of consensus on best practices, and by the never-completed final report of the National Commission on Offsets.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: The report is GAO-08-854, issued June 26, 2008, and is 36 pages. The DPA was reauthorized through September 30, 2008. DOD places priority ratings on approximately 300,000 contracts annually. Since 2003, DHS reported that it authorized or endorsed the use of priority ratings 15 times, with over half in support of critical infrastructure protection and restoration requirements. Since late 2003, Commerce reported it has taken approximately 180 actions to provide Special Priorities Assistance. The most recent annual report on offsets, issued December 2007, noted that its analysis does not include the potential effects of nearly $1 billion of technology transfer, training, and overseas investment offset transactions, representing nearly 24 percent of average annual offset transactions. The 2004 subcontractor report covered nearly 700 weapon systems and components contracts for 1998 through 2002, requested documentation for only two weapon systems from each of the 13 U.S. prime contractors, and had a less than 40 percent response rate to the survey of three tiers of subcontractors. Currently, 84 percent of the value of export contracts involving offsets submitted by prime contractors is for the aerospace industry. Offset regulations require reporting for offset agreements exceeding $5 million in value. DHS reported it could take 21 to 50 days to establish a voluntary agreement following a disaster. In 2002, DOT obtained a priority rating to support procurement of approximately 1,800 Explosives Detection Systems machines for U.S. airports by December 31, 2002. DOD proposed amendments to DPA including reducing the waiting period for awarding contracts from 60 to 30 days and increasing the statutory limitation on Title III actions from $50,000,000 to $200,000,000. Title III projects have ranged from $88,000 to approximately $164 million, with a total of $449.3 million shown in Table 2. Figure 1 shows the number of Title III projects initiated by fiscal year: 2002, 1 DOD-initiated and 0 congressionally requested; 2003, 1 and 0; 2004, 0 and 2; 2005, 5 and 3; 2006, 1 and 6; 2007, 2 and 4; and 2008, 0 and 7.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The document recommends that the Secretaries of Agriculture, Health and Human Services, and Transportation, in consultation with the Department of Commerce, develop and implement a system for using the priorities and allocations authority for food and agriculture resources, health resources, and civil transportation respectively. It recommends that the Secretaries of Agriculture, Energy, Health and Human Services, Homeland Security, and Transportation consider, in advance of an emergency, approving programs and placing priority ratings on contracts for items likely to be needed in an emergency. It recommends that the Secretary of Commerce update regulations to, for example, request more specific industry information from prime contractors that would improve the assessment of the economic effects of offsets. The document also reports that USDA generally concurred with the findings and recommendations, and that HHS and DOT indicated in technical comments that they will implement the recommendations.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The document states that it is difficult to isolate the effects of offsets from the numerous other factors affecting specific industry sectors. It notes that Commerce's annual offset report analysis does not include the potential effects of nearly $1 billion of offset transactions, and that Commerce officials said their analysis could be improved by requesting more detailed sector and product information. The interagency team chaired by DOD reached consensus with foreign nations that adverse effects of offsets exist, but not yet on best practices to address them, and participating nations noted that producing a preliminary statement by the latter half of 2008 will be difficult and time-consuming. The National Commission on Offsets produced an interim report in 2001, but its final report and recommendations were never produced. The document notes that events that would trigger use of some Title VII authorities, such as the National Defense Executive Reserve and voluntary agreements, have not occurred, and that some agencies lack policies, guidance, or timelines for completing regulations. It also notes that BIS is conducting a review of data and methodology, but that changes to the regulation would not affect data collection for the next annual report.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This is a U.S. Government Accountability Office report to Congress, dated July 31, 2008, on the Trans-Sahara Counterterrorism Partnership (TSCTP), the primary vehicle of U.S. counterterrorism policy in northwestern Africa. It examines (1) the distribution of funds for TSCTP in 2005 through 2008 and the types of activities supported, and (2) the program's implementation, including the extent to which it has been guided by a comprehensive, integrated strategy. It covers nine partner countries in the Sahel, Maghreb, and sub-Saharan regions and the activities of the Department of State, USAID, and the Department of Defense.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: GAO found that in 2005 through 2008, the key agencies distributed the majority of TSCTP resources to countries in the Sahel region, supporting a range of diplomacy, development assistance, and military activities. In 2005 through 2007, about 74 percent of approximately $230 million obligated went to Chad, Mali, Mauritania, and Niger. GAO also found that several challenges hampered implementation: no comprehensive, integrated strategy had been developed to guide the program; disagreements between State and DOD about whether State should have authority over DOD personnel temporarily assigned to conduct TSCTP activities contributed to the suspension of some activities; fluctuation in the distribution of funds limited USAID's implementation of activities in Mali, including suspension of a peace-building program in northern Mali; and the agencies had few common mechanisms for measuring outcomes, generally not measuring results such as any decrease in extremism in targeted regions.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: Since the program's inception, the key agencies' obligations and commitments for TSCTP amounted to about $353 million. In 2005 through 2007, the agencies obligated about $230 million; for 2008, commitments totaled approximately $123 million. Of the 2005 through 2007 obligations, about 74 percent went to Chad, Mali, Mauritania, and Niger; about 3 percent to Algeria, Morocco, and Tunisia; about 8 percent to Nigeria and Senegal; and the remaining 15 percent to regional assistance. As of June 2008, the agencies expected to distribute about 49 percent of 2008 commitments to the Sahel, 21 percent to the Maghreb, 13 percent to sub-Saharan countries, and 17 percent to regional assistance. By year, DOD obligations and commitments were $7 million in 2005, $39 million in 2006, $118 million in 2007, and $92 million in 2008; State and USAID obligations and commitments were $18 million in 2005, $10 million in 2006, $37 million in 2007, and $31 million in 2008. By country, 2005 through 2007 obligations and 2008 commitments were: Chad $23 million and $9 million, total $32 million; Mali $31 million and $6 million, total $37 million; Mauritania $18 million and $6 million, total $24 million; Niger $37 million and $7 million, total $44 million; Algeria $1 million and $6 million, total $7 million; Morocco $3 million and $6 million, total $9 million; Tunisia 0 and $1 million, total $1 million; Senegal $9 million and $3 million, total $12 million; Nigeria $3 million and $5 million, total $8 million; and regional assistance $22 million and $10 million, total $30 million. In addition, $147 million was obligated for program support costs for all TSCTP partner countries. For State and USAID TSCTP activities by country and year, the obligations were: Chad $2,780,000 in 2005, $2,990,000 in 2006, and $2,895,000 in 2007; Mali $2,330,000 in 2005, $550,000 in 2006, and $13,570,000 in 2007; Mauritania $2,620,000 in 2005, $58,000 in 2006, and $6,200,000 in 2007; Niger $3,220,000 in 2005, $4,340,000 in 2006, and $5,372,000 in 2007; Algeria $417,876 in 2005, 0 in 2006, and 0 in 2007; Morocco $1,550,000 in 2005, $463,381 in 2006, and $382,423 in 2007; Tunisia 0 in 2005, $32,836 in 2006, and 0 in 2007; Nigeria 0 in 2005, 0 in 2006, and $1,260,000 in 2007; Senegal $397,000 in 2005, $1,160,000 in 2006, and $3,970,000 in 2007; and regional assistance $5,000,000 in 2005, 0 in 2006, and $3,650,000 in 2007. USAID worked with the United Nations Development Program to reintegrate more than 3,000 ex-rebel fighters into civil society in Niger.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: GAO recommends that the Secretary of State work through the Director of Foreign Assistance, who serves concurrently as USAID Administrator, to develop a comprehensive strategy for the Trans-Sahara Counterterrorism Partnership in conjunction with the Secretaries of Defense and the Treasury, the U.S. Attorney General, and the heads of any other participating agencies; the strategy should include clear goals, objectives, and milestones, including output and outcome indicators, and identify resources needed to achieve the program's goals. GAO also recommends that the Secretaries of State and Defense develop and issue joint guidance with regard to DOD personnel temporarily assigned to conduct TSCTP activities in the partner countries. State and USAID concurred with the findings and recommendations; DOD partially concurred, stating that sufficient guidance exists in governing statutes and directives, while GAO maintains that joint guidance is needed to resolve existing disagreements.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The report states that there is no central repository for TSCTP funds and that the funding data were collected and maintained with some limitations, although GAO concluded the data were sufficiently reliable for the report's objectives. It also states that no comprehensive, integrated strategy had been developed as of June 2008; that disagreements between State and DOD over authority could not be resolved at the country level and required higher-level guidance or intervention; that none of the nine partner countries' country action plans had been approved by ambassadors as of June 2008, and only Niger and Mauritania had held country-level CAP discussions; and that the agencies had not yet developed common indicators to measure outcomes, with officials noting the difficulty of measuring how activities such as building wells or providing radios contribute to TSCTP goals. The report also notes that the 2004 and 2005 planning documents do not prioritize proposed activities, identify milestones, provide guidance for selecting countries, or determine when countries no longer require assistance. GAO states it plans to issue a classified annex to this report.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This document is a U.S. Government Accountability Office report to congressional committees, issued August 22, 2008, titled 'Chemical Safety Board: Improvements in Management and Oversight Are Needed.' It examines how the Chemical Safety and Hazard Investigation Board (CSB) has responded to GAO and inspector general recommendations regarding its investigative gap, data quality, human capital, and accountability and management problems, and assesses the merits of the current oversight approach using an existing inspector general versus alternative approaches. It makes recommendations to CSB and proposes matters for congressional consideration.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The findings are GAO's own. The document finds that CSB has implemented some GAO and IG recommendations but has not fully addressed several critical recommendations, and problems in governance, management, and oversight persist. The investigative gap persists: using fiscal year 2002 data, the DHS IG reported that CSB deployed to 4 of 294 accidents that met statutory criteria, and in fiscal year 2007 CSB investigated 1 of approximately 35 accidents with at least one fatality, and less than 1 percent (5 of 920) of accidents of which it was notified. Data quality problems continue: CSB has not issued the required reporting regulation, relies primarily on media sources, and GAO found at least five accidents (about 6 percent of cases reviewed) where fatalities were not correctly recorded and seven accidents (about 4 percent of cases reviewed) where injury data were missing. Human capital problems persist: more employees left CSB in fiscal years 2006 and 2007 than were hired, three of five investigators who left were senior investigators with 5 to 7 years of experience, and CSB has not paid a retention bonus to any employee since September 2002. Accountability and management problems continue: CSB lacks a permanent chief operating officer. GAO concludes that independent oversight from an existing inspector general remains the most effective way to help CSB address its continuing problems, provided the arrangement is made permanent and funding is provided to the IG for the function.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: The document reports the following figures: CSB received notification of approximately 900 chemical accidents in calendar year 2007, and 31 of these accidents were serious or even fatal events warranting CSB investigators. CSB received an appropriation of $9.4 million for fiscal year 2008 and had 39 staff as of January 30, 2008. Since fiscal year 2001, three IGs made 32 recommendations to CSB. Using fiscal year 2002 data, the DHS IG reported in fiscal year 2004 that CSB deployed to 4 of 294 accidents that met statutory criteria. In fiscal year 2007, CSB received notifications of 920 chemical accidents; approximately 35 of these accidents included at least one fatality, and CSB investigated 1 of these. Also in fiscal year 2007, CSB investigated less than 1 percent (5 of 920) of accidents of which it was notified. In fiscal year 2006, CSB recorded 822 total accidents, deployed to 9, investigated 6, had 38 accidents with fatalities, and investigated 5 of those; in fiscal year 2007, CSB recorded 920 total accidents, deployed to 8, investigated 5, had 35 accidents with fatalities, and investigated 1 of those. NTSB's budget is approximately 8 times CSB's budget, and NTSB investigates 250 times as many accidents. In fiscal year 2006, CSB initiated 6 investigations with a budget of $9.1 million, while NTSB initiated 1,521 aviation accident investigations with a budget of $75.9 million. In a subset of database cases, GAO found at least five accidents (about 6 percent of cases reviewed) where fatalities were not correctly recorded, and seven accidents (about 4 percent of cases reviewed) where injury data were missing. In fiscal years 2006 and 2007, more employees left CSB than were hired; 3 of 5 investigators who left were senior investigators with 5 to 7 years of experience, and 4 of 11 staff hired were investigators, 3 of them interns. CSB has not paid a retention bonus to any employee since September 2002. In fiscal year 2006, CSB reprogrammed compensation funds of $627,891 to other priorities, and in fiscal year 2007, it reprogrammed compensation funds of $407,383. CSB's prior appropriations and staff levels include fiscal year 2008, $9.4 million and 39 staff; fiscal year 2006, $9.2 million and 41 staff; fiscal year 2004, $8.2 million and 40 staff; and fiscal year 2000, $8.0 million and 27 staff. For fiscal year 2009, CSB requested $10.6 million and 47 staff; in fiscal year 2000, CSB requested $12.5 million and 60 staff.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: GAO recommends that the chairman of the Chemical Safety Board develop a plan to address the investigative gap and request the necessary resources from Congress to meet CSB's statutory mandate or seek an amendment to its statutory mandate; consider using the work of other entities, such as government agencies, companies, and contractors, subject to an assessment of the quality of their work, to a greater extent to maximize the board's limited resources; improve the quality of its accident-screening database by better controlling data entry and periodically sampling accident data to evaluate their consistency and completeness; publish a regulation requiring facilities to report all chemical accidents, as required by law; consider reinstating the position of chief operating officer, with delegated responsibility for establishing performance goals, holding program managers accountable for meeting those goals, and demonstrating improvement in the agency's ability to meet its statutory mandates over time; and use the Strategic Management of Human Capital portion of the President's Management Agenda to provide criteria for developing a comprehensive human capital plan, with input from investigators, that includes specific objectives and performance measures. GAO also proposes matters for congressional consideration: Congress may wish to consider amending CSB's authorizing statute or the Inspector General Act of 1978 to permanently give EPA's Inspector General the authority to serve as the oversight body for CSB, and providing the EPA Inspector General with appropriations and staff allocations specifically for the audit function of CSB via a direct line in the EPA appropriation.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The document states that GAO did not evaluate the quality of CSB's investigative products issued to date, or the quality and effectiveness of its reports, recommendations, and promotion of preventive actions, because those evaluations were outside the scope of the mandate. It also did not conduct a detailed evaluation of the oversight arrangements for the other 53 federal entities for comparison with CSB. The document notes limitations in CSB's accident-screening database, including the lack of quality controls to ensure that data are accurate and complete, especially with respect to fatalities, and that totals of accidents and accidents with fatalities may be underestimated. The document also reports that CSB disagreed with GAO's interpretation that the law requires investigation of all accidental releases that result, or have the potential to result, in a fatality, serious injury, or substantial property damage; CSB stated it would work with Congress to clarify its statutory mandate and, if appropriate, seek an amendment, while GAO continued to believe the current law is clear. The document further notes that NTSB nonaviation investigations were excluded from the 1,521 total because the data were not available in the source.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This GAO report, mandated by Congress, examines the federal tax incentives under the Gulf Opportunity Zone Act of 2005 that state and local governments were responsible for allocating and overseeing in Alabama, Florida, Louisiana, Mississippi, and Texas. It identifies the four incentives, describes the states' allocation processes and compliance monitoring, and reports how much of each incentive was used and for what purposes as of mid-June 2008 and April 2008.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The document finds that the GO Zone Act of 2005 made state governments responsible for allocating four tax incentives: $14.9 billion in tax-exempt private activity bond authority, $330 million in low-income housing tax credits, $350 million in GO Zone tax credit bonds, and $7.9 billion in additional advance refunding bonds. Alabama, Louisiana, and Mississippi generally allocated bond authority on a first-come, first-served basis, while all five eligible states used existing procedures to award LIHTCs. As of mid-June 2008, the three eligible states had allocated about 87 percent of the private activity bond authority, but bonds had been issued for only about half of the awarded authority, reflecting 44 percent of the total. As of April 2008, the five states had awarded 95 percent of the LIHTC allocation, but few planned LIHTC units were in service. The states used the debt relief provisions to varying degrees: Louisiana and Mississippi exhausted the $350 million tax credit bond authority, Alabama issued none, and the three states used 16 percent of the advance refunding authority. State officials identified challenges including reduced credit availability, declining tax credit values, and difficulty identifying eligible debt.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: Under the GO Zone Act of 2005, the states were responsible for allocating $14.9 billion in tax-exempt private activity bond authority, $330 million in low-income housing tax credits, $350 million in GO Zone tax credit bonds, and $7.9 billion in additional advance refunding bonds. As of mid-June 2008, the three eligible states had allocated about 87 percent of the $14.9 billion bond authority, and bonds issued amounted to about 44 percent of the total authority; the 10 largest bonds issued accounted for approximately 92 percent, 76 percent, and 69 percent of total bonds issued in Alabama, Louisiana, and Mississippi, respectively. As of April 2008, the five eligible states had awarded 95 percent of the $330 million in LIHTCs; planned units were 3,259 in Alabama, 226 in Florida, 11,787 in Louisiana, 9,301 in Mississippi, and 398 in Texas, while in-service units were 68, 0, 2,156, 328, and 0, respectively. GO Zone LIHTC-funded units will address 17 percent of rental housing units with major or severe hurricane damage in Louisiana and 45 percent in Mississippi. Louisiana issued $200 million and Mississippi issued $100 million of GO Zone tax credit bonds, exhausting their $350 million authority; Alabama issued none. As of mid-June 2008, the three states had issued additional advance refunding bonds accounting for 16 percent of their total allocation authority: Alabama had issued $599 million, or about 53 percent; Louisiana had issued $483 million, or about 11 percent; and Mississippi had issued $169 million, or about 8 percent.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: Not stated in this document.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The document states that it did not attempt to quantify aggregate bond use by categories across states because of differences in the way bond type data were reported. Comparable data on rental housing units with major or severe damage were not available for every GO Zone parish and county in Louisiana and Mississippi, or for Alabama, Florida, or Texas. The document also notes that it did not assess the extent to which LIHTC monitoring policies have been followed because few GO Zone LIHTC-funded units had been placed in service as of April 2008. It further notes that state officials were uncertain whether GO Zone bonds should be used quickly anywhere in the qualified areas or focused more on the most damaged areas, and that some counties and parishes may have benefited from projects affecting multiple counties even if they had no specific allocations.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This document is a July 31, 2008, GAO follow-up audit report to the Subcommittee on Oversight and Investigations, Committee on Veterans' Affairs, House of Representatives. It assesses the Department of Veterans Affairs' progress in strengthening controls over information technology (IT) equipment, including implementation of GAO's 2004 and 2007 recommendations, and the effectiveness of VA's current internal controls to prevent theft, loss, or misappropriation of IT equipment. It covers VA's 2007 departmentwide physical inventory and GAO's tests at four case study locations: North Texas, Puget Sound, and Boston health care systems, and VA headquarters.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: VA made significant progress in addressing prior GAO recommendations: as of July 2008 it had completed action on 10 of 12 recommendations from GAO's July 2007 report and 4 of 6 property-related recommendations from GAO's July 2004 report, with partial or planned action on the rest. VA's 2007 departmentwide physical inventory initially identified approximately 79,000 missing IT equipment items; as of May 15, 2008, OIT reported approximately 62,800 recorded items could not be located, of which over 9,800 could have stored sensitive information. GAO's statistical tests at four case study locations, conducted February through May 2008, identified continuing control weaknesses: 50 missing items, including 34 that could have stored sensitive information, plus blank serial numbers, inaccurate user organization and location information, and other recordkeeping errors. Estimated missing-item failure rates were 1 percent at Puget Sound HCS, 3 percent at Boston HCS, 6 percent at North Texas HCS, and 12 percent at VA headquarters. GAO also found weaknesses in controls over hard drives in the disposal process and physical security weaknesses at IT storage locations, and found that medical equipment with data storage capability was not included in VA's physical inventory of IT equipment.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: Key figures in the report include: approximately 79,000 missing items initially identified by VA's 2007 departmentwide inventory; approximately 62,800 recorded items not located as of May 15, 2008; over 9,800 of those could have stored sensitive information. The table in the report gives totals of 62,880 missing items and 9,866 open Reports of Survey items that could have stored sensitive data. VA had over 43,000 items listed on open Reports of Survey as of May 15, 2008. GAO's tests identified 50 missing items, 34 of which could have stored sensitive information. Estimated missing-item failure rates were 1 percent at Puget Sound HCS, 3 percent at Boston HCS, 6 percent at North Texas HCS, and 12 percent at VA headquarters. GAO estimated incorrect user organization rates of 91 percent at North Texas, 60 percent at Boston, 76 percent at Puget Sound, and 12 percent at VA headquarters; incorrect user location rates were 46 percent, 17 percent, 14 percent, and 33 percent respectively. North Texas had a 59 percent actual blank serial number rate. VA completed 10 of 12 recommendations from GAO's 2007 report and 4 of 6 property-related recommendations from GAO's 2004 report, and the report makes 5 recommendations.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The document recommends that the Secretary of Veterans Affairs require the CIO, with the support of tested medical centers and VA headquarters organizations and other VA organizations, to take five actions: review property inventory records and confirm that all IT equipment, regardless of organizational equipment inventory listing, is identified in the property system; establish and implement a policy requiring development of standardized naming classifications for IT equipment, including item name, manufacturer, and model, for recording into local property inventory systems; develop a list of medical equipment with data storage capability that should be considered as IT equipment for inventory control purposes; develop a procedure for identifying hard drive serial numbers with both property identification numbers and serial numbers of host computers; and revise the definition of IT storage locations in VA Handbook 0730/1 to include informal IT storage locations, such as OIT work rooms, and require these locations to be included in physical security inspections. VA officials said they agreed with the intent of all five recommendations after follow-up clarification.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The report states that VA does not know what, if any, sensitive information resided on missing equipment or when the equipment was lost, so notifications to potentially affected individuals could not be made in accordance with OMB guidance. Because VA facilities had not always documented IT equipment disposal for many years, there was no way to determine whether missing items were lost or stolen. The lack of user-level accountability and inaccurate records make it difficult to determine the extent to which actual theft, loss, or misappropriation may have occurred. The report did not validate VA's departmentwide inventory results, and states the numbers of missing items could be higher because not all IT equipment was included in the inventory, such as medical equipment with data storage or processing capabilities and items recorded to other equipment inventory listings. VA officials could not tell GAO the quantity of IT equipment items not included in the four case study populations.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This is a U.S. Government Accountability Office report, GAO-08-925, issued July 31, 2008, about rebaselining of major federal information technology projects. It examines how many of the federal government's major IT projects have been rebaselined, the reasons for rebaselining, and whether the 24 major federal agencies have sound rebaselining policies. It also makes recommendations to the Office of Management and Budget and the heads of the 24 major agencies.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The report's own survey found that an estimated 48 percent of the federal government's major IT projects have been rebaselined, 51 percent of rebaselined projects were rebaselined at least twice, and about 11 percent were rebaselined four or more times. The most commonly cited reason for rebaselining was changes in project requirements, objectives, or scope, reported 55 percent of the time, followed by changes in funding stream, reported 44 percent of the time. The report found that all 24 major agencies have rebaselining policies, but none of the policies were fully consistent with the five best practices in GAO's Cost Assessment Guide. It also found that OMB has not issued guidance specifying what elements agency rebaselining policies should include.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: The federal government planned to spend about $70 billion on IT projects in fiscal year 2008, including 778 major projects among the 24 major agencies. GAO surveyed a random sample of 180 projects and achieved a 99 percent response rate. GAO estimated that 48 percent of major IT projects had been rebaselined, while figure 1 in the report displays 49 percent rebaselined and 51 percent not rebaselined. Of rebaselined projects, 51 percent were rebaselined at least twice and about 11 percent were rebaselined four or more times. Reasons for the most recent rebaseline, with percentages of times reported, were: change in project requirements, objectives, or scope, 55 percent; change in funding stream, 44 percent; original baseline was inaccurate, 14 percent; cost or schedule overruns due to project performance, 4 percent; cost or schedule overruns due to contractor performance, 4 percent; and other, 41 percent. The report cites cost and schedule changes for previously reviewed projects in millions of dollars: National Polar-orbiting Operational Environmental Satellite System, original cost $7,000, cost after rebaseline $12,500, dollar change $5,500, percent change 79 percent, original completion date 2018, completion date after rebaseline 2026, delay 8 years; Navy Enterprise Resource Planning, original cost $1,993, cost after rebaseline $2,445, dollar change $452, percent change 23 percent, original completion date Jun. 2011, completion date after rebaseline Aug. 2013, delay 2.2 years; FAA Standard Terminal Automation Replacement System, original cost $940, cost after rebaseline $2,770, dollar change $1,830, percent change 195 percent, original completion date Oct. 2005, completion date after rebaseline Dec. 2007, delay 2.2 years; FAA Wide Area Augmentation System, original cost $1,001, cost after rebaseline $3,340, dollar change $2,339, percent change 234 percent, original completion date Aug. 1999, completion date after rebaseline Dec. 2008, delay 9.3 years; U.S. Coast Guard Rescue 21, original cost $250, cost after rebaseline $711, dollar change $461, percent change 184 percent, original completion date 2006, completion date after rebaseline 2011, delay 5 years. The report also gives policy assessment figures: 14 policies (58 percent) fully addressed describing reasons when a rebaseline is warranted, 5 (21 percent) partially, and 5 (21 percent) not addressed; 0 (0 percent) fully addressed describing the process for developing a new baseline, 13 (54 percent) partially, and 11 (46 percent) not addressed; 5 (21 percent) fully addressed requiring validating the new baseline, 6 (25 percent) partially, and 13 (54 percent) not addressed; 9 (38 percent) fully addressed requiring management review, 14 (58 percent) partially, and 1 (4 percent) not addressed; and 6 (25 percent) fully addressed requiring that the process is documented, 15 (63 percent) partially, and 3 (13 percent) not addressed.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The report recommends that the Director of OMB issue guidance for rebaselining policies that would include a minimum set of key elements, taking into consideration the criteria used in the report. It also recommends that each of the heads of the 24 major agencies direct the development of comprehensive rebaselining policies that address the weaknesses GAO identified.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The document states that all survey results are estimates from a sample and have 95 percent confidence intervals within plus or minus 11 percentage points, unless otherwise noted. It notes that OMB has not issued guidance specifying what elements agency rebaselining policies should include, and that OMB officials acknowledged they have not established specific criteria to evaluate earned value management policies, including their rebaselining aspects. The document also describes disagreements with its assessments: the Department of Homeland Security disagreed that its policy addressed none of the practices, but did not provide the guidance GAO requested, so GAO did not reconsider its ratings; the Departments of Commerce and Defense disputed the use of NPOESS as an example of a rebaselined IT project, and GAO modified the report to acknowledge that the departments do not include the entire NPOESS program in their IT reporting. The document also notes that some agencies provided additional documentation that led GAO to change some assessments.

audience.name: Who it is for
audience.text: It is for the congressional requesters, particularly the Subcommittee on Federal Financial Management, Government Information, Federal Services, and International Security of the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs, and for OMB, the 24 major agencies, and other interested parties overseeing federal IT investments.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This GAO report (GAO-08-930, issued September 10, 2008) examines Department of Defense planning for the reposturing of U.S. forces from Iraq, focusing on the logistical organizations and processes that would support a drawdown, especially the retrograde of materiel and equipment. It determines (1) the extent to which logistical planning has begun and the assumptions upon which it is based, and (2) whether DOD has established roles and responsibilities for managing and executing the retrograde of materiel and equipment from Iraq, and it identifies issues DOD will need to consider as it develops a comprehensive plan for reposturing.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The report finds that various defense commands began planning for reposturing in fall 2007, but initial efforts by the Army Materiel Command, the Defense Logistics Agency, and Headquarters, Department of the Army were uncoordinated and lacked a joint perspective. Planning efforts were synchronized by May 2008 through a logistics summit at Camp Arifjan, Kuwait, and MNF-I published a logistics reposture order. DOD's planning is based on three key assumptions: any reposturing will be based on MNF-I and Department of State assessments of conditions on the ground; there will be sufficient lead time to refine plans once an order with a specific timetable and force posture is issued; and reposturing will be deliberate and gradual, predicated on a 180-day process for units leaving Iraq and a sustained flow of no more than 2.5 brigades' worth of equipment and materiel out of Iraq each month. The report also finds that DOD, CENTCOM, and the military services have not clearly established roles and responsibilities for managing and executing retrograde. There is no unified or coordinated structure accounting for the theater property and retrograde support teams, the designated executive agent lacks necessary authority, ARCENT did not have command authority over the two Army field support brigades responsible for the bulk of retrograde until June 2008, and data systems used during retrograde are incompatible. The report identifies nine issues DOD needs to consider: management of hazardous materials and waste and property disposition during base closures; reposturing of contractors; accountability and disposition of contractor-managed government-owned property; restrictive conditions on facilities in Kuwait and neighboring countries; availability of wash racks and customs inspectors; capacity of transportation and convoy security assets and route limits; increased demand for mental health care providers; infrastructure requirements of returning units; and requirements for training and equipment reset. DOD has begun to address these issues, but none have been fully addressed.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: As of April 26, 2008, there were approximately 149,400 DOD contractors and, as of July 1, 2008, approximately 147,400 U.S. troops deployed in support of Operation Iraqi Freedom. DOD officials reported that these forces were located on approximately 311 installations, with some installations more than 500 miles from Kuwait. Approximately 80 percent of the equipment used by U.S. troops in Iraq is theater provided equipment. As of March 2008, the pool of theater provided equipment totaled approximately 173,000 major end items worth approximately $16.5 billion. As of May 2008 there were the equivalent of 47 brigades' worth of materiel and equipment in Iraq, with approximately 582,000 pieces of theater provided equipment worth about $15.5 billion. As of summer 2007 there were more than 60,000 materiel containers in Iraq and over 127,000 short-tons of ammunition in Iraq and Kuwait. On May 16, 2008, 177 pieces of theater provided equipment rolling stock were sitting idle in Kuwait, and over 2,100 non-rolling stock items were also sitting idle. There are 211 wash racks in Kuwait: 81 at Camp Arifjan and 130 at Kuwait Naval Base, of which only 100 are useable because the remaining 30 lack necessary filters. Larger vehicles can take from 40 to 80 hours to clean, while smaller vehicles take 4 to 8 hours. Manifest information does not reach the field support brigade until 24 to 48 hours after a vessel sets sail. There is at least $3.5 billion worth of contractor-managed government-owned property in Iraq, with $3.37 billion under LOGCAP. The donation threshold for excess U.S.-owned personal property in Iraq was increased from $5,000 to $10,000 in October 2007 and from $10,000 to $15,000 in June 2008. The Army's analysis indicates that approximately 85 percent of contractor-acquired government-owned property in Iraq should be transferred, sold, or scrapped in Iraq, while the remaining 15 percent can be sold or reused elsewhere. Marine Corps officials reported they could retrograde only 20 to 30 percent of their nonsensitive materiel through one alternate port. It takes 1 to 2 months to close the smallest installations, and ARCENT officials estimate it could take longer than 18 months to close a complex installation such as Balad Air Force Base, which contains approximately 24,000 inhabitants. Officials from the 1st Cavalry Division said it would be 6 to 9 months after returning from Iraq before their brigade combat teams would have the necessary equipment with which to train.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The report recommends that the Secretary of Defense, in consultation with CENTCOM and the military departments, take steps to clarify the chain of command over logistical operations in support of the retrograde effort, addressing not only the Army field support brigades but also the theater property and retrograde support teams. It also recommends that the Secretary of Defense, in consultation with the military departments, correct the incompatibility weaknesses in the various data systems used to maintain visibility over equipment and materiel while they are in transit. The report presents a matter for congressional consideration: Congress may wish to consider directing DOD to include in its briefings submitted in accordance with the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2008 specific details on the status of its reposturing planning and how it intends to mitigate specific reposturing issues, including those identified in the report, as well as other challenges the department envisions as it proceeds with its reposturing efforts. DOD partially concurred with the first recommendation and fully concurred with the second.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The report states that the pace and overall extent of reposturing has yet to be determined. It also states that, as of May 2008, there was no agreed-upon definition for retrograde as it applies to reposture planning. DOD officials and GAO analysis indicate that the rate-of-flow model should not be used to predict how long it would take to retrograde all the equipment and materiel in Iraq because actual amounts vary by brigade and several identified issues are not currently accounted for by the model. According to ARCENT officials, time and costs for closing installations are difficult to estimate without a bilateral agreement between the United States and Iraq on base closure, and as of July 18, 2008, no such agreement existed. The report notes that CENTCOM's June 2008 action giving ARCENT operational control over the 401st and 402nd Army Field Support Brigades may result in changes, but GAO had not yet evaluated the effect of that change. ARCENT had not received the authorities it requested as of May 2008. As of June 2008, DCMA officials stated that they were not aware of a theater-wide plan for the reposturing of contractors. The report says the Army Sustainment Command order to fix the data incompatibility problem has not been implemented for reasons that were not made clear. It also notes that wash rack restrictions at Kuwait Naval Base could occur more often if the retrograde of ammunition were accelerated, and that additional customs inspectors would be necessary if the pace of retrograde increased. The report says home station issues need to be explored further, and that DOD has begun to address the identified issues but none have been fully addressed.

audience.text: The report is addressed to the congressional committees, specifically the Senate and House Armed Services Committees and the Senate Appropriations Subcommittee on Defense, to support congressional oversight of DOD's planning for reposturing U.S. forces from Iraq.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This document is a September 2008 U.S. Government Accountability Office report to the Ranking Member of the House Committee on Veterans' Affairs. It examines the Department of Veterans Affairs' progress in reducing underutilized and vacant property, how much VA spends to operate and maintain that property, how VA has used legal authorities such as enhanced-use leases and sharing agreements to reduce such property, and what challenges remain. The scope covers VA property data for fiscal years 2005 through 2007, site visits at eight VA medical facilities plus a Veterans Benefits Administration facility and a national cemetery, and an independent cost estimate of operating and maintaining underutilized and vacant VHA space.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: VA made significant progress reducing underutilized space, from 15.4 million square feet in fiscal year 2005 to 5.6 million square feet in fiscal year 2007, so that underutilized space fell from about 10 percent of VA's total square feet to less than 4 percent. Vacant space remained relatively unchanged, totaling about 7.3 million square feet in fiscal year 2007 and accounting for about 5 percent of total square feet in all three fiscal years. GAO estimated that VA spent $175 million in fiscal year 2007 operating and maintaining underutilized and vacant space at its medical facilities, although VA itself does not track these costs at the building level. VA's use of authorities such as enhanced-use leases and sharing agreements likely contributed to reductions, but VA does not track the overall effect of these authorities on space reductions. Ongoing challenges include building location, high repair costs, historic designation, competing stakeholder interests, and legal and budgetary restrictions, though some VA locations have used stakeholder outreach and public-private partnerships to mitigate these challenges. VA concurred with two of GAO's three recommendations but did not concur with the recommendation to collect and maintain building-level data by fiscal year.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: From fiscal year 2005 through 2007, VA reduced underutilized space from 15,374,292 square feet to 5,591,257 square feet, a reduction of approximately 64 percent; VA reported 9,795,006 underutilized square feet in fiscal year 2006 and 2,513 underutilized buildings in fiscal year 2006 and 2,381 in fiscal year 2007. Vacant square feet were 7,367,340 in fiscal year 2005, 7,635,489 in fiscal year 2006, and 7,297,407 in fiscal year 2007, with 684 vacant buildings in fiscal year 2006 and 482 in fiscal year 2007. GAO estimated VA spent $175 million in fiscal year 2007 operating and maintaining underutilized and vacant VHA space, with an estimated range of $175 million to $185 million at the 50 percent and 70 percent confidence levels, and about $481,000 each day. Ninety-eight percent of underutilized and vacant space was at VHA facilities. VA has more than 32,000 acres of land, over 6,200 buildings on approximately 300 sites; VHA operated 144.6 million square feet including 155 hospitals, 881 outpatient clinics, 135 nursing homes, 46 residential rehabilitation treatment programs, and 207 readjustment counseling centers; VBA operated 4.3 million square feet; NCA operated 972,000 square feet of building space and 17,000 acres at 125 national cemeteries and 33 soldiers' lots. In fiscal year 2007, 56 percent of buildings in poor or critical condition were underutilized or vacant, with repair costs estimated at approximately $3 billion; 66 percent of underutilized and vacant buildings are historic or eligible for historic designation; 29 percent of underutilized and vacant properties require repairs costing a minimum of $1 million per building and 7 percent require more than $5 million per building. VA reported approximately 46 enhanced-use leases, 185 sharing agreements, and 250 outleases in fiscal year 2007, with the total number of authorities remaining around 475. From fiscal years 2005 through 2007, VA disposed of 91 buildings through enhanced-use leases, demolished 98 buildings, sold or donated 5 buildings, and disposed of 6 through GSA. In fiscal year 2007, VA spent $3,449,568 demolishing 44 buildings totaling 216,952 square feet. Examples include a Chicago enhanced-use lease that brought $28 million on execution and an additional $22 million on later sale, totaling $50 million; Los Angeles filming agreements generating roughly $1 million to $2 million a year; a North Chicago cell tower sharing agreement providing about $40,000 annually; an energy center saving VA $4 million per year; and about $8 million in recorded revenue from all agreements in fiscal year 2007. VHA had 2,716 available acres in fiscal year 2007, up from 2,356 acres in fiscal year 2005. Also in fiscal year 2007, 97 percent of underutilized buildings assessed had a component in poor or critical condition, 99 percent of vacant buildings had such a component, 68 percent of underutilized buildings were aged 51 years or older, and 89 percent of vacant buildings were aged 51 years or older.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The report recommends that the Secretary of Veterans Affairs take three actions: develop an annual cost estimate for how much VA spends on underutilized and vacant property so that the estimate is comprehensive, accurate, well-documented, and credible; collect and maintain building-level data by fiscal year in order to correlate characteristics associated with underutilized and vacant buildings, which may help identify unneeded assets; and track, monitor, and evaluate square footage reductions and financial and nonfinancial benefits when recording new agreements as of fiscal year 2008. The document notes that VA concurred with the first and third recommendations but did not concur with the recommendation on collecting and maintaining building-level data.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The document states that because VA did not maintain building-level data before fiscal year 2006, GAO could not determine building-level trends in underutilized and vacant space for fiscal years 2005 through 2007, and that the fiscal year 2006 and 2007 snapshots were not comparable. It also states that VA does not track operations and maintenance costs on a building-by-building basis and has not developed a reliable method for estimating these costs, which is why GAO conducted its own estimate. The document says VA does not track the overall effect of its legal authorities on space reductions, so the extent of their contribution is unknown, and VA's data systems limit the ability to compare agreements and identify resulting reductions. GAO found instances of missing agreement data, indicating that the roughly $8 million revenue figure for fiscal year 2007 may actually be higher. The document also notes that GAO's site visit sample was a nonprobability sample and cannot be statistically projected to VA as a whole. Finally, the document reports that VA did not concur with one recommendation and raised five areas of disagreement, including that the report double-counted vacant space and overstated unit costs, and that GAO revised its estimate in response.

audience.text: This report is addressed to the Honorable Steve Buyer, Ranking Member of the House Committee on Veterans' Affairs, to provide information on VA's progress in reducing underutilized and vacant property and the challenges to VA's efforts.
