about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This document is a U.S. Government Accountability Office report to congressional requesters, GAO-08-954, issued July 28, 2008 (48 pages), titled 'Electronic Health Records: DOD and VA Have Increased Their Sharing of Health Information, but More Work Remains.' It describes the Department of Defense and Department of Veterans Affairs progress in developing electronic health record systems or capabilities that allow full interoperability of personal health care information, steps the departments have taken to comply with federal interoperability standards, implementation specifications, and certification criteria, and efforts to establish the joint interagency program office required by the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2008. The report covers the period of the audit, March through July 2008.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: GAO found that DOD and VA have established and implemented mechanisms to share some, but not all, electronic health information, and that the information is shared at different levels of interoperability. Outpatient pharmacy and drug allergy data on shared patients are exchanged in computable form, the highest level, while other data, such as microbiology results, cytology reports, and chemistry and hematology reports, are viewable only. Not all electronic health information is shared; examples include immunization records and history, data on exposure to health hazards, and psychological health treatment and care records. VA's health information is all electronic, but not all DOD health data are electronic because many DOD medical facilities use paper-based records. DOD and VA have agreed on numerous common standards, including standards in current and emerging federal interoperability specifications, and are participating in federal standards initiatives. The joint interagency program office is still in early stages: leadership positions are not permanently filled, staffing is incomplete, facilities are not designated, and the required implementation plan remains in draft with many milestone dates undetermined. GAO concluded that without a fully established program office and finalized implementation plan, the departments may be challenged in meeting the September 2009 deadline for interoperable electronic health records and capabilities.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: The report is GAO-08-954, a 48-page report issued July 28, 2008. DOD and VA have been working to exchange patient health data electronically since 1998. A May 2003 presidential task force recommended bidirectional electronic health records by fiscal year 2005. The National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2008 required systems or capabilities allowing full interoperability by September 30, 2009. As of June 2008, outpatient pharmacy and drug allergy data were being exchanged on more than 18,300 shared patients. The Laboratory Data Sharing Interface is deployed at nine locations. The departments endorsed 20 sets of standards under the Consolidated Health Informatics initiative. An April 2004 executive order called for widespread adoption of interoperable electronic health records by 2014. The American Health Information Community is an 18-member federal advisory body. HITSP examined more than 700 existing standards and identified 30 named standards. The American Health Information Community developed seven use cases in 2006 and 2007 and is developing six use cases for 2008. In 2006, the Certification Commission certified the first 37 ambulatory electronic health record products; to date it has certified over 100 products. The Office of the National Coordinator released a four-year strategic plan in June 2008. The first release of the CHDR interface was implemented at one site in September 2006. BHIE completed an interface with DOD's Clinical Data Repository in July 2007, and viewable patient vital signs sharing through BHIE began in June 2008. Viewable inpatient data from CIS are available at 17 DOD sites (about 40 percent of inpatient beds) and all VA sites. FHIE transfers text data from DOD to VA weekly if a discharged patient has been referred to VA for treatment, otherwise monthly. AHLTA version 3.3 was conditionally certified in April 2007 against 2006 outpatient electronic health record criteria and is installed at three DOD locations for beta testing. The Acting Director and Acting Deputy Director of the joint interagency program office were appointed April 17, 2008; the office is expected to number about 30 staff. $4.94 million was requested to fund the office for fiscal year 2008, expected to be received in July, and $6.94 million for fiscal year 2009 was submitted in June. The draft implementation plan was dated April 25, almost 2 months after the February 28, 2008 due date. Interoperability I milestones are due September 2008; the first milestone, sharing vital signs information, has been achieved. Interoperability II is to be completed by September 2009, but of 52 milestone dates, 19 are yet to be determined. VA expects to appoint a permanent Deputy Director by October 2008 and hire permanent program staff by December 2008. The departments expect to identify milestones and timelines by October 31, 2008. The Joint Clinical Information Board is expected to identify data types and formats by July 31, 2008, and the Health Executive Council is to approve data elements by August 31, 2008.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: GAO recommends that the Secretaries of Defense and Veterans Affairs give priority to fully establishing the Joint Interagency Program Office by expediting efforts to put in place permanent leadership, staff, and facilities, and to make the necessary decisions to finalize the draft implementation plan. The report notes that both departments concurred with the recommendations.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The report states that DOD and VA cannot yet share all essential health information, and that not all electronic health information is shared; examples are immunization records and history, data on exposure to health hazards, and psychological health treatment and care records. It also states that many DOD medical facilities use paper-based health records, and that clinical encounters for TRICARE enrollees are not captured in DOD's electronic health system unless care is received at a military treatment facility. The report notes that computable health data are exchanged only for shared patients who have been activated, and that officials are unable to track the number of shared patients currently receiving care from both departments, so the potential number is unknown. BHIE inpatient data are available only from a portion of DOD inpatient hospitals, not all military hospitals. The DOD/VA Information Interoperability Plan is still in draft, with 19 of 52 Interoperability II milestone dates not yet determined, and decisions on those dates depend on clinical priorities, technical considerations, and policy decisions; the plan is intended to be a living document. The report says it has not assessed the draft plan, and no decision on a joint inpatient system had been made as of the report. The Office of the National Coordinator's June 2008 strategic plan has not been fully assessed. AHLTA version 3.3 cannot be fully certified until it has been verified in operational use at a medical site. The report also notes that federal standards continue to evolve and that the National Coordinator said it would not be advisable for DOD and VA to move significantly ahead of the national standards initiative. The exchange of psychological health records requires policy decisions regarding appropriate access.

audience.text: This report is addressed to the congressional committees that requested it, including the defense and military construction appropriations subcommittees and the Armed Services and Veterans' Affairs committees of the Senate and House of Representatives, and it is intended to support congressional oversight of DOD and VA interoperability efforts.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This is a U.S. Government Accountability Office report, GAO-08-976, issued September 2008, reviewing whether the design of the Veterans Health Administration's internal controls over the use of miscellaneous obligations was adequate for fiscal year 2007. It describes how VHA used miscellaneous obligations, principally approximately $6.9 billion for mission-related goods and services, and whether VA's policies and procedures provided adequate controls over their authorization and use.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The report's own findings are that VHA used miscellaneous obligations extensively in fiscal year 2007: according to IFCAP data, VHA made approximately $6.9 billion in miscellaneous obligations, with about $3.8 billion, or 55.1 percent, for fee-based medical and dental services and another $1.4 billion, or 20.4 percent, for drugs, medicines, and hospital supplies. The report found that VA policies and procedures were not designed to provide adequate controls over oversight by contracting officials, segregation of duties, and supporting documentation. In 42 case-study obligations, all 42 lacked documented approval by contracting officials, 30 had inadequate segregation of duties, 20 had blank vendor fields, 16 had blank contract fields, and 8 had incomplete purpose descriptions. The report also found that the IFCAP database lacked vendor information for over 88,000, or 69 percent, of 127,070 miscellaneous obligations, accounting for over $5 billion of the $6.9 billion. It found that new guidance issued in May 2008 offered some improvement but did not fully address the three problem areas, and that the guidance had not been subject to legal review.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: In fiscal year 2007, IFCAP data show VHA made 127,070 miscellaneous obligations totaling $6.9 billion, which was 70 percent of the total dollar value, while VA's Central Office made 4,839 obligations totaling $2.9 billion, which was 30 percent; the combined total was 131,909 obligations and $9.8 billion. The VHA total was composed of $3,805 million, or 55.1 percent, for services; $1,412 million, or 20.4 percent, for supplies; $628 million, or 9.1 percent, for rent, communications, and utilities; $553 million, or 8 percent, for state homes and homeless veteran support; $301 million, or 4.4 percent, for transportation of persons and things; and $210 million, or 3 percent, for other items. In the case studies, 42 miscellaneous obligations totaled $36,045,896: Pittsburgh had 14 obligations totaling $6,694,853, Cheyenne had 11 totaling $2,076,648, and Kansas City had 17 totaling $27,274,395. The report also identified 145 miscellaneous obligations for over $30.2 million that appeared to be used to procure items such as passenger vehicles, furniture and fixtures, office equipment, and medical, dental, and scientific equipment. VHA officials had earlier disclosed that $4.8 billion, or 56 percent, of the reported $8.6 billion in procurements through the third quarter of fiscal year 2007 had been done using funds categorized as miscellaneous obligations.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The report recommends that the Secretary of Veterans Affairs, in conjunction with VA's Office of General Counsel, develop and implement policies and procedures consistent with federal appropriations law and internal control standards that: establish a process for the review of miscellaneous obligations by contracting officials, including requiring appropriate documentation that the review has occurred; segregate duties for creating, approving, and recording miscellaneous obligations, for the certification and payment of invoices, and for the receipt of the resulting goods or services; document the purposes, vendors, and contract numbers of miscellaneous obligations; and establish an oversight mechanism to ensure that these control policies and procedures are fully and effectively implemented. The report states that VA concurred with these recommendations and identified specific actions it planned to take.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The report states that its case-study results are illustrative and nongeneralizable because the 42 miscellaneous obligations reviewed cannot be projected to the overall population of miscellaneous obligations in fiscal year 2007. It did not review VHA's procurement or service authorization processes, and it could not reconcile IFCAP miscellaneous obligations to VA's Financial Management System because FMS does not identify the method used to obligate funds. The report also states that the work was not designed to identify fraudulent or otherwise improper purchases or to estimate their full extent, and it found no examples of fraudulent or otherwise improper purchases. It could not confirm that VHA was properly billed for livers or that the procurement was properly authorized because officials could not provide the contract or the standardized pricing schedule. It did not verify that VHA officials were properly following the Medicare fee schedule formula for payments to non-VA physicians. It also notes that VA attorneys had not reviewed the new miscellaneous obligations policies to help ensure compliance with applicable appropriations law and other requirements, and that the May 2008 guidance did not address segregation of duties or establish an oversight mechanism.

audience.text: This report is addressed to the Chairman and Ranking Member of the Subcommittee on Oversight and Investigations, Committee on Veterans' Affairs, House of Representatives, to support the Subcommittee's oversight of VHA's financial management and use of miscellaneous obligations.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This document is a U.S. Government Accountability Office report (GAO-08-981R, issued August 15, 2008) prepared for four congressional committees. It examines the Department of Defense's programs to promote positive working relationships between reservists and their employers: whether DOD has informed reservists of their obligations to notify employers of active-duty calls, what initiatives DOD has developed to promote positive relations, and whether there has been a reduction in hiring of reservists since September 11, 2001. It makes recommendations to the Secretary of Defense.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The document finds that DOD has taken steps to inform reservists of their USERRA obligations and responsibilities to their employers, but it does not collect data to assess the effectiveness of those efforts. It finds that the amount of advance notice reservists provide to employers varies and that some reservists in focus groups said they planned to give no more than 30 days notice regardless of how much notice they received from DOD. It finds that DOD has used ESGR as its focal point for a strategic approach with many outreach initiatives, but ESGR lacks an established annual performance plan, a follow-up mechanism for maintaining employer relationships after statements of support are signed, and an outreach program specific to small businesses. The document also finds that it was unable to determine whether there has been a reduction in hiring of reservists since September 11, 2001, because of a lack of available data. DOD partially concurred with the three final recommendations.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: The document's notable figures include: more than 650,000 members of the National Guard and Reserve used since September 11, 2001; ESGR's fiscal year 2008 budget of approximately $13.1 million; ESGR's workforce of 36 military employees, 28 civilian employees, 8 contractors, and 94 contractor field support personnel; more than 4,500 volunteers in 56 committees; in fiscal year 2007, more than 67,000 employers and approximately 235,000 reservists were briefed on USERRA and ESGR services; in the 2006 Status of Forces Survey, an estimated 79 percent of responding reserve component members said they had been briefed on USERRA at least once; in the 2007 Status of Forces Survey, an estimated 76 percent of reservists had received an informal alert notice, an estimated 77 percent of those received notice of 30 days or more, and an estimated 47 percent of reservists received written, formal orders 30 days or more before reporting; ESGR field committees briefed 68,803 employers in fiscal year 2007; 15,124 employers were nominated for the Patriot Award in fiscal year 2007; more than 1,000 reservists nominated their employers for the Freedom Award in fiscal year 2007; more than 20,644 employers signed statements of support in fiscal year 2007; a November 2007 DOD report found that nearly 70 percent of employers of selected reservists have fewer than 100 employees; a strategic-plan goal seeks statements of support from 100 percent of identified employers by 2011, equating to an average of 20 percent per year; ESGR sent direct mail about itself to 250,000 Society for Human Resource Management members and to 15,700 International Association of Chiefs of Police members; on January 19, 2007, DOD changed from a 24-month cumulative involuntary mobilization limit to a maximum of 12 months at a time; the focus groups comprised 10 focus groups in three states with 50 volunteer participants; 77 employers were randomly selected and 11 interviews were completed. DOD's comments cite ESGR Ombudsman contacts of 5,298 in fiscal year 2005, 7,765 in fiscal year 2006, 13,116 in fiscal year 2007, and 8,575 in fiscal year 2008 as of June 30; actual cases of 4,682, 3,152, 2,374, and 1,988 in the same periods; and statements of support of 10,909, 11,396, 20,644, and 27,770 in those fiscal years as of June 30.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The document recommends that the Secretary of Defense direct the Under Secretary of Defense for Personnel and Readiness to take three actions: establish an annual performance plan that develops and facilitates implementation of performance measures on how well ESGR is achieving its goals; conduct regular and recurring follow-up activities on outreach efforts to maintain positive working relationships with employers who have previously signed statements of support; and develop initiatives to specifically conduct outreach efforts to small businesses that employ reservists. The document also states that a fourth draft recommendation, to add questions to DOD's Status of Forces Surveys about the amount and form of notice reservists give their employers, was omitted from the final report because Defense Manpower Data Center officials said they plan to include such questions, and GAO encourages full implementation of that initiative.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The document states that it was unable to determine the extent to which there has been a reduction in the hiring of reservists caused by the increase in the use of reservists after September 11, 2001, or caused by changes in DOD policies, due to a lack of available data, and that no studies or analyses from DOD or the Department of Labor were identified. It further states that even if a reduction had occurred, it would be unable to determine what factors contributed. The report notes that its focus groups and structured employer interviews were based on nonprobability samples and are not generalizable to the population of reservists or reservist employers. It also states that DOD does not know the effectiveness of its notification efforts because it does not collect data on the amount or form of notice reservists provide, and that ESGR does not know the extent to which its outreach initiatives help achieve its mission because it lacks a performance plan, a follow-up mechanism, and a small-business outreach program. It notes that it is difficult to establish a direct causal link between ESGR's numerous outreach efforts and their effectiveness.

audience.name: Who it is for
audience.text: This document is addressed to the congressional committees named in the Military Reservists and Veteran Small Business Reauthorization and Opportunity Act of 2008: the Senate Committee on Armed Services, the Senate Committee on Small Business and Entrepreneurship, the House Committee on Armed Services, and the House Committee on Small Business, to support their oversight of DOD's reservist-employer relations programs.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This report, a public version of the restricted report GAO-08-453SU, examines TSA's requirements for domestic air carriers to conduct watch-list matching—comparing passenger data to the No Fly and Selectee lists—for domestic flights, and the extent to which TSA has assessed air carriers' compliance with those requirements. It covers TSA's security directives, its inspection process, the January 2008 special emphasis inspection, and TSA's expectation that the Secure Flight program will be the ultimate solution.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: TSA has issued two security directives, one for the No Fly List and one for the Selectee List, that require air carriers to match passenger data, including identifying similar-name matches. Before the April 2008 revision, the directives were broad and did not specify how many or what types of name variations air carriers must compare, and the 14 air carriers interviewed reported varied approaches, so a passenger could be identified as a match by one carrier and not another. TSA had conducted limited testing of similar-name-matching capability until a January 2008 special emphasis inspection found deficiencies: no air carrier successfully identified matches involving all types of name variations, though TSA gained confidence in air carriers' exact-name matching. In April 2008 TSA revised the No Fly List security directive to establish a baseline similar-name-matching capability to which all air carriers must conform, and planned to revise the Selectee List directive similarly; TSA officials called this an interim solution and said Secure Flight, expected to begin implementation in 2009, is the longer-term solution. During fiscal year 2007, TSA conducted 1,145 watch-list-related inspections and found compliance in 1,133 (99 percent), but testing of similar-name matching was limited and done at inspectors' discretion without baseline evaluation criteria. TSA began corrective actions and planned new inspection guidance, but it was too early to determine the extent of future compliance assessments.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: The report states that, as of January 2008, nine principal security inspectors were responsible for assessing compliance of domestic air carriers, and as of June 2008, 681 transportation security inspectors were responsible for 459 commercial airports. For fiscal year 2007, there were 72 domestic air carriers to which the directives applied. TSA conducted 1,145 watch-list-related inspections in fiscal year 2007: 1,109 by transportation security inspectors and 36 by principal security inspectors; the inspections covered 60 of the 72 carriers, and TSA found compliance in 1,133 (99 percent) of the 1,145 inspections. Documentation referred to name-matching tests in 55 of the 1,109 transportation security inspector inspections and in 6 of the 36 principal security inspector inspections; 6 of the 9 principal security inspectors said their assessments had not included examining certain basic types of similar-name comparisons. The 14 air carriers interviewed accounted for approximately 70 percent of passengers boarding domestic flights in 2005; 10 of the 14 reported that more similar-name comparisons result in more potential matches, and 12 of the 14 said large numbers of potential matches can cause congestion and longer waits. The January 2008 special emphasis inspection was a 3-day inspection using 100 No Fly List names to test 83 air carriers (52 domestic and 31 foreign). TSA conducted a special emphasis assessment during May 20–29, 2008, of seven air carriers' compliance. TSA officials said air carriers would need 2 to 4 weeks to implement the revised directive's requirements, and that a third-party vendor option could take almost 2 years. TSA expects Secure Flight to begin assuming watch-list matching in early calendar year 2009. The document also notes more than 6 years passed after September 11, 2001, and a 3-year period from January 2005 through December 2007 for documented incidents.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: Not stated in this document.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The document states that it is too early to determine the extent to which TSA will assess air carriers' compliance with the revised requirements because its efforts are still underway. It also states that data on false negative watch-list-matching results generally are not available for domestic flights, so the extent to which domestic air carriers may be failing to identify watch-listed individuals is difficult to determine. The report notes that the 2005 special emphasis assessment cannot produce a reliable estimate of the success rate of all attempted matches because sampling was not random; that the results of the 14-carrier interviews are not generalizable to all domestic air carriers; and that GAO did not independently verify each air carrier's reported method, did not independently assess the sufficiency of the new baseline capability, and did not assess the reliability of data from the January 2008 special emphasis inspection or the May 2008 special emphasis assessment. TSA officials acknowledged the new baseline does not address all possible types of name variations or all vulnerabilities identified by TSA, and Secure Flight still faced challenges including cost and schedule estimates. Details of the May 2008 assessment are classified.

audience.name: Who it is for
audience.text: The report is addressed to the congressional committees that requested the review, including committees and subcommittees of the U.S. Senate and House of Representatives responsible for appropriations, commerce, transportation, homeland security, judiciary, and oversight; it supports congressional oversight of TSA's watch-list matching and Secure Flight implementation.
